Epidemiology of Chikungunya Virus Infection in the Philippines.
Background: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) has circulated in the Philippines for more than six decades. We systematically reviewed the epidemiology of CHIKV in the Philippines, integrating evidence on transmission, seroprevalence, diagnostics and molecular lineages. Methods: We searched PubMed and Embase to March 2026 for original studies reporting incidence, prevalence, seroprevalence, outbreak characteristics, or surveillance findings in human populations in the Philippines. The gray literature from the Department of Health (DOH) Epidemiology Bureau's national chikungunya surveillance (2018-March 2026) was included separately. Findings were synthesized narratively because of substantial heterogeneity. Results: Sixteen studies and one national surveillance dataset were included. National surveillance recorded 12,662 cases from 2018 to early 2026, including 722 laboratory-confirmed cases and three fatalities. The Asian genotype predominated during the 2011-2013 epidemic, while Indian Ocean lineage (IOL) viruses were detected in southern Mindanao. Conclusions: Transmission of CHIKV in the Philippines is mostly sporadic with periods of low-level transmission. Tempered fractional rabies dynamics with deep neural surrogate modeling: Analysis, computation, and prediction.
Rabies is a fatal zoonotic disease for which domestic dogs constitute the main reservoir; its long and variable incubation period motivates transmission models that account for memory effects. This paper proposes a tempered fractional rabies model in which the classical time derivative is replaced by the left tempered Caputo derivative of order ξ ∈ (0, 1] and tempering parameter λ ≥ 0, so that the dynamics remain nonlocal while the influence of past states decays exponentially. We first establish the qualitative properties of the model: solutions remain nonnegative for nonnegative initial data, total populations are bounded on finite time intervals, and a unique continuous solution exists, which we prove by combining an exponential transformation with a contraction argument. We further derive the basic reproduction number R0 by the next-generation-matrix approach and prove local asymptotic stability of the disease-free equilibrium whenever R0<1, uniformly in the fractional order and the tempering parameter. A predictor-corrector product-integration scheme is then developed for the tempered system, and a mesh-refinement study confirms an empirical convergence order close to one. To accelerate repeated simulations, we train a deep neural surrogate that maps a short history window of log-transformed states to log-state increments, using a two-stage procedure consisting of one-step pretraining followed by differentiable rollout fine-tuning. Ablation experiments show that the logarithmic state representation and the increment-based targets are the decisive design choices, while rollout fine-tuning further improves worst-case robustness of free-running predictions. The selected surrogate attains high one-step accuracy (RMSE 0.4121, MAE 0.1303, R2=0.999998) and, in fully free-running closed-loop mode, reproduces unseen tempered test scenarios with mean R2=0.9990 (mean RMSE 3.32) on the benchmark cases and R2=0.9973±0.0031 over a random evaluation suite of 18 unseen tempered scenarios; accuracy degrades only in the near-untempered long-memory limit λ → 0, which we characterize explicitly. Parameter-matched LSTM and GRU baselines trained under the identical protocol do not outperform the proposed feed-forward surrogate, and in batched operation the surrogate is about two orders of magnitude faster than the numerical solver. The resulting framework provides a fast, accurate, and stable proxy of the tempered fractional rabies model that supports rapid parameter sweeps and forecasting-oriented scenario analysis.

From mapping to prediction: A systematic review and critical appraisal of methodological approaches to assessing avian influenza incursion risk in domestic poultry.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) viruses continue to threaten global poultry production and public health. To examine how methodological approaches have been used to assess this risk, we conducted a systematic review and critical appraisal of peer-reviewed studies assessing avian influenza virus (AIV) incursion risk in domestic poultry, using PubMed and Web of Science databases. Quantitative modelling approaches ranged from statistical, data-driven methods to mechanistic frameworks and operated at different spatial and temporal scales, using farms or geographical areas as the epidemiological unit of interest. Across studies, analytical choices were largely shaped by data availability, which constrained achievable resolution and influenced the questions models could address. Most applications focused on area-level analyses, often describing historical spatial risk patterns rather than supporting prospective inference. Statistical models frequently relied on proxy variables linked to past incursions, limiting biological interpretability and robustness. Recent improvements in wild bird surveillance, including citizen-science initiatives, have enabled more explicit representation of wild bird dynamics, although persistent gaps in poultry population data continue to restrict model development in many settings. In settings where farm-level data are limited, mechanistic approaches are commonly applied, relying on assumptions regarding underlying disease transmission dynamics. A consistent challenge across studies was limited model validation, reflecting sparse outbreak data and spatial and temporal clustering of outbreaks. Interpretation was further complicated by scale mismatches and risks of ecological and atomistic fallacies when extrapolating between farm-level and area-level outputs. Overall, the review highlights the importance of ensuring that risk questions and predictive expectations reflect the available data and the feasibility of validation.

National memory path study: Formation of register-based cohorts of persons diagnosed with dementia in Finland in 2019 and 2021.
AIMS: This study describes the study design and methodology for the formation of novel National Memory Path cohorts, outlined to investigate dementia incidence and health and social service use preceding dementia diagnosis in Finland before and after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, and to enable further national-level analyses. METHODS: A register-based study was conducted, consisting of all Finnish home-dwelling adults who received a dementia diagnosis in 2019 or 2021. Dementia was defined based on the diagnosis in the Finnish Health Care Registers, or on the prescription of an anti-dementia drug in the Finnish Prescription Centre. Health and social service use within 12 months before the diagnosis included visits to outpatient and inpatient care in primary and secondary healthcare, emergency departments and home care recorded in the Finnish Health Care Registers. RESULTS: Altogether, 23,121 and 22,419 persons were diagnosed with dementia in 2019 and 2021, respectively, corresponding to an incidence of 520 and 501 per 100,000 in mean population. The highest number of diagnoses occurred in the 75-84 age group. Within 12 months before the diagnosis, 98% had used health and social services. Outpatient care in primary healthcare was the most often used service, followed by outpatient care in secondary healthcare and emergency department use. CONCLUSIONS: National health registers enable comprehensive analysis of dementia incidence and service use. Frequent service use prior to the dementia diagnosis creates opportunities for dementia symptom detection across various parts of the health and social care system.

Exploring the role of COVID-19 pandemic preparedness in Norway's Ukrainian refugee crisis response.
AIMS: The aim of this study was to explore how and in what ways COVID-19 preparedness in Norway shaped the organization and delivery of the country's response to the Ukrainian refugee crisis and identify lessons learned from the overlap of the pandemic and the refugee crisis to strengthen Norway's preparedness for future crises, as perceived by the participants. METHODS: A qualitative study with in-depth, semi-structured, individual interviews was conducted among 10 individual, civil society, and government actors who worked in relation to both the COVID-19 pandemic and the Ukrainian refugee crisis. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis. RESULTS: The following four themes emerged, including both positive and negative consequences of the end of the pandemic overlapping with the beginning of the Ukrainian refugee crisis: (1) pandemic-shaped mindsets and momentum in crisis response, (2) adapting pandemic resources for refugee crisis response, (3) participation and power in crisis decision-making, and (4) lessons learned: continuity is key. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides an enhanced understanding of how selected Norwegian actors perceived the role of COVID-19 preparedness in the Ukrainian refugee crisis response. Participants identified both strengths, such as the reuse of resources and coordination structures, and challenges related to communication and participation in decision-making. Understanding these experiences may help inform future preparedness planning across overlapping crises.

Adaptive Governance and Community Agency in Crisis: A Qualitative Study of Stakeholder Engagement in Seke District, Zimbabwe.
The COVID-19 pandemic caused serious problems all across the world, particularly in places with little resources like Seke District of Zimbabwe. With an emphasis on adaptive governance, community agency, and crisis management, this qualitative study sought to investigate stakeholder contributions and views of community engagement in the COVID-19 pandemic response within Seke District. Thirty purposefully sampled stakeholders, including government officials, health professionals, traditional and religious leaders, and representatives of non-governmental organisations, participated in semi-structured interviews as part of a qualitative approach. Thematic analysis was then used to pinpoint important themes pertaining to community engagement, community participation, stakeholder engagement strategies and results. During the COVID-19 pandemic in Seke District, community engagement involved hybrid communication networks that combined conventional means with digital platforms like WhatsApp. The legitimacy of public health initiatives was greatly aided by local and religious players. Adaptive resource allocation to vulnerable populations was facilitated by community-based data systems and participatory planning. Despite enduring obstacles like inadequate infrastructure, digital exclusion, false information, and socioeconomic weaknesses, the results included increased health literacy, improved stakeholder collaboration, improved disease control, and livelihood modifications. In Seke District, Zimbabwe, the study emphasises the significance of trusted local leadership and context-specific community engagement in pandemic response. These results offer important insights into successful stakeholder engagement strategies in low-resource environments during the COVID-19 epidemic, providing lessons for similar health emergencies in the future.

New WHO technical package to help countries improve health data for COVID-19 response and beyond
Today, as part of its commitment to strengthening health information systems and improving health[1], especially in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO announced a new approach to improving access to life-saving data: the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the urgent need for timely and reliable data to drive strategic health action. Too many countries still lack both the infrastructure to routinely gather health data and the analytical capacity to use these data for effective health actions and emergency response. “Countries must be able to measure progress to make progress,” said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. “Particularly during COVID-19, reliable data is the best way to coordinate response efforts and improve health in all areas.” Accurate health data are necessary to understand specific country needs in order to improve health and save lives. Data also helps direct scarce resources to where they are needed most. The SCORE (Survey, Count, Optimize, Review, Enable) Technical Package aims to improve the availability of timely, reliable, validated, and comparable health data. For the first time in a single, harmonized package, it represents all the key elements for optimized health information system performance. Simply put, SCORE will help governments around the globe set benchmarks and improve standards in healthcare. In response to the challenges of data availability highlighted in the WHO World Health Statistics 2020 report, SCORE includes more than 90 universally-accepted tools and standards for health information systems strengthening. “Using data to inform public health priorities and strategies has never been more important,” said Dr Kelly Henning, Director of Public Health Programs at Bloomberg Philanthropies[2]. “The SCORE Technical Package provides country governments around the world with high-quality, essential technical guidance so that countries can strengthen their own data systems.” WHO is proud to partner with the Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative to deliver this timely resource to countries. Below are some examples of how SCORE can improve individual lives and communities: The birth of a child is registered so they can access essential health services, attend school, and apply for a passport; A death is registered with cause-of-death accurately captured so that policy-makers have a better understanding of all-cause and COVID-specific mortality and associated risk factors and implement programs and policies to save lives; Health data are disaggregated by age, sex and cause of death to illustrate the root causes of health disparities and help direct resources to the most vulnerable groups such as those who do not speak the local language or face stigma and discrimination in their community; Health facilities have the capacity to regularly measure the quality of their services, workforce and patient data and can make a compelling case for increased funding to national and international stakeholders; Health data are integrated with other sectors so that social determinants of health such as pollution, sanitation and nutrition are addressed to reduce the overall burden of disease. The package's initial release includes two documents: SCORE Essential Interventions – including an overview of health information systems, underlying elements, and indicators to assess progress with sample actions; and SCORE Tools and Standards -- including resources to address critical health data gaps and strengthen country health data. “We must keep score to save lives. WHO is committed to working with countries and partners to rapidly scale up capacity for data collection and use in order to improve policy and performance,” added Dr Samira Asma, Assistant Director-General for Data, Analytics and Delivery for Impact at WHO. “We must act now to invest in statistical systems in countries, respond to this pandemic and meet the SDGs and the Triple Billion targets. Our window of opportunity is closing, and we cannot wait to address data gaps. Data use to address country needs has to be a priority today.” Country-owned, disaggregated data will be essential for more resilient and sustainable health systems going forward. COVID-19 is both a wake-up call and a stark reminder of the challenges we still have to address. But it is also an opportunity to build back better through solidarity, information-sharing and collaboration. SCORE is one example of how a collaborative approach can benefit countries by providing a common set of tools based on shared standards. This package is designed to be practical, actionable and flexible. We will only be successful in combatting COVID-19 if we work together. Future components of the SCORE Technical Package are due to be released later this year, including the SCORE Assessment Instrument and global, regional and country status reports. Together, these will provide a complete package of information to plan and monitor progress against national and subnational priorities as well as global targets. ----- [1] https://www.who.int/about/what-we-do/thirteenth-general-programme-of-work-2019---2023#:~:text=The%20Thirteenth%20General%20Programme%20of,health%20at%20the%20country%20leve [2] Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative provided funding to support the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package

The Quadripartite organisations (FAO, UNEP, WHO and WOAH) highlight country action, science and investment as priorities for advancing One Health at the 9th World One Health Congress in Lisbon, Portugal. The Quadripartite partners – the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) – highlighted a shared focus on implementation, science and investment at the 9th World One Health Congress , held in Lisbon, Portugal, from 4 to 7 September, 2026. Across the joint sessions, the partners explored how stronger country implementation, scientific evidence and investment can help realise tangible One Health outcomes, supported by intersectoral collaboration, and reflecting the interconnectedness between the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems. A key focus was implementation of the One Health Joint Plan of Action (OHJPA) at country level. Discussions at a session on the OHJPA explored how countries are translating the global framework into national action, while identifying practical enablers and barriers to implementation. Representatives from Singapore, Malawi and Uzbekistan shared their experiences of implementing One Health approaches, including their use of the OHJPA and its implementation guide developed by the Quadripartite. These experiences provided practical perspectives on how cross-sectoral coordination can be strengthened and adapted to national contexts. The Quadripartite partners at the One Health Congress. The partners also highlighted the importance of science and evidence in guiding One Health action. During its second term, the One Health High-Level Expert Panel (OHHLEP) has generated evidence and recommendations to support countries and partners in implementing One Health. During the Congress, OHHLEP presented its 10 recommendations addressing barriers, strengthening enabling conditions and advancing implementation. At the Congress, OHHLEP also presented its mapping of international instruments for One Health, examining how One Health is reflected in sector-specific global normative instruments, and identifying opportunities for greater coherence, collaboration and action. Bringing this work into the Congress discussions reinforced the role of strategic scientific advice in shaping effective One Health policies and action. At the Congress, investment and financing formed a third key strand of Quadripartite engagement. Sessions explored how to build the investment case for One Health, demonstrate return on investment and identify opportunities to mobilize resources, including through blended financing. A session jointly organised with the World Bank further explored approaches to financing One Health action. With over 1, 300 participants, the 9th World One Health Congress brought together researchers, policymakers, practitioners and other stakeholders from around the world to advance One Health science, policy and practice. Together, the joint sessions demonstrated the Quadripartite’s commitment to helping countries move from global commitments to practical action, underpinned by evidence and supported by sustainable investment. WOAH calls on its Members to strengthen surveillance, early warning and preparedness for vector-borne diseases (VBDs). A vector-borne disease is a disease that can be transmitted from one animal or person to another through a living organism, known as a vector. Vectors are most often insects, such as mosquitoes, ticks, fleas or sandflies, which can carry and transmit pathogens. Analysis of official reports submitted through the World Animal Health Information System (WAHIS) shows a steady increase of the frequency (incidence) of some of these VDBs and the overall number of countries reporting these diseases. Vector-borne diseases are currently showing a marked change in global distribution, with climate change acting as an important driver, alongside anthropogenic factors, vectors ecology, ecological disruption, higher mobility of animals and humans. Analysis of official information reported through WAHIS indicates a marked increase in reported exceptional epidemiological events for several VBDs with important implications for animal health, biodiversity conservation, food security, livelihoods and the resilience of Veterinary Services worldwide. A marked rise since 2023 Data reported through WAHIS reveal a marked rise in VBDs notified to WOAH through WAHIS from 2023 onward, concentrated in a small number of diseases and countries. Bluetongue accounts for the largest amount of this increase, with an average of 38 exceptional epidemiological events per year recorded in 2023–2025 compared with an average of 9.1 events per year between 2015 and 2022 — driven mainly by the incursion of the BTV-3 serotype into north-western Europe beginning in autumn 2023. West Nile fever (a zoonosis that can cause encephalitis in humans) events increased substantially from 8.0 per year on average to 55 per year. Equine infectious anemia showed more moderate increase, led by an increase in reporting of cases in countries in the Americas. By contrast, other listed vector-borne diseases, including lumpy skin disease , have generally remained close to their historical baseline in term of number of exceptional epidemiological events, but have significantly increased their geographic range from Africa to Middle East, Europe and Asia. Since 2005, bluetongue alone has accounted for the majority of all VBD outbreaks reported to WOAH, with lumpy skin disease the next most frequently reported. Regional patterns vary considerably. Since 2022, Europe has reported the overwhelming majority of bluetongue outbreaks, while Africa has remained the primary region affected by Rift Valley fever, and the Americas have accounted for the majority of equine infectious anemia and western equine encephalitis cases. These data should be interpreted as trends in reported events , rather than as a direct measure of changes in disease incidence. Changes in surveillance intensity, diagnostic capacity and notification practices can influence reporting alongside genuine changes in disease occurrence and distribution. Climate change as a structural driver The observed trends are consistent with the demonstrated relationship between climate change and vector ecology highlighted in WOAH’s 2025 State of the World’s Animal Health report . Rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns and land-use modifications are altering vector density, activity periods, survival and geographical range. In some areas, conditions may allow vectors to reproduce throughout the year, substantially extending their activity period and increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission. These changes can create conditions favourable to the establishment or transmission of VBDs into previously unaffected, often temperate, regions. WOAH reporting has documented changes in the geographical distribution of several VBDs, including an increase in the maximum latitude at which outbreaks have been reported. Other factors—including ecological change, unregulated animal movements and trade, and changes in wildlife–livestock–human interactions—can also influence VBD emergence and spread. Many of the vectors involved pathogens that affect both animals and humans, reinforcing the need for surveillance and response that spans the animal–human–environment interface. Some vector-borne diseases involve complex interactions between animals, humans, vectors and the environment. Effective prevention and control require an integrated One Health approach involving Veterinary Services, public health authorities, environmental agencies, research institutions and other relevant stakeholders. Control options may be limited, with vaccination being an effective measure where available. Other preventive measures include reducing vector breeding sites, using mechanical protection and, where appropriate, repellents. Environmental insecticide use should be carefully considered due to potential impacts on non-target organisms and ecosystems. Continued research is also needed to develop and evaluate biological control approaches. WOAH’s international standards — including the Terrestrial Code recommendations on surveillance for arthropod vectors — provide the scientific foundation for Members to assess vector presence, distribution and abundance, and to design surveillance strategies proportionate to risk. WOAH also supports its Members through innovative early-warning approaches. Since 2022, the PROVNA project has worked with Veterinary Services in North Africa to combine earth observation and climate data with disease occurrence data reported through WAHIS. The project is building models capable of identifying areas with environmental and climatic characteristics suitable for VBDs presence and transmission. Such approaches demonstrate how transdisciplinary collaboration between epidemiologists, entomologists, data scientists and Veterinary Services can shift disease response from reactive to anticipatory. WOAH calls on its Members to: Strengthen integrated surveillance and early warning , combining vector, disease and environmental data to detect changes in distribution, abundance and transmission risk at an early stage before they escalate; Report vector-borne disease events promptly and transparently through the World Animal Health Information System (WAHIS), including relevant information on serotypes and strains where available; Invest in entomological, laboratory and diagnostic capacity , including within national Veterinary Services and in collaboration with WOAH Reference Centres, to sustain vector monitoring and disease surveillance over the long term; Adopt risk-based, science-based control measures , including timely vaccination with quality-assured and epidemiologically appropriate vaccines, vector control and movement management, adapted to the local ecology and epidemiological situation; Strengthen cross-sectoral and cross-border collaboration , including through regional networks and initiatives such as PROVNA, GF-TADs, VectorNet, MediLabSecure among others and the Quadripartite One Health activities, to anticipate and respond to vectors that do not recognise national boundaries; and Facilitate safe trade through science-based measures , ensuring that import risk management measures are proportionate to the identified risk and consistent with WOAH International Standards. As several factors mentioned above continue to reshape the ecology of disease vectors, investment in surveillance, laboratory capacity and Veterinary Services is essential not only for animal health but also for food security, livelihood, biodiversity protection, as well as global health security. WOAH remains committed to supporting its Members through its international standards, expert networks, data systems and scientific collaboration to anticipate, prevent and respond to vector-borne disease evolving threat. Spectroscopic and computational studies on biophysical aspects of ivermectin binding with human hemoglobin: thermodynamics and structural insights.
Proteins are known to play multifunctional role including transportation, storage, structural support among others. Among the proteins, hemoglobin (Hb) is known to transport oxygen and binds with many xenobiotics and therapeutic drugs. But, in this paper, the binding of human hemoglobin (HHb) with Ivermectin (IVM) that is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic agent used during COVID-19 pandemic has been presented. Multi-spectroscopic experimental techniques and in-silico docking methods have been used for the intended study. IVM quenched HHb fluorescence via a dynamic quenching process with a quenching constant (Ksv) on the order of 105 M- 1. TCSPC studies confirmed the dynamic quenching by showing a decrease in the lifetime of the fluorophore (HHb) in presence of IVM. The binding affinity (Kb) from UV-Vis and fluorescence studies was on the order of 105 M- 1. The binding constant was observed to increase with rise in temperature. Thermodynamic parameters of the interaction (ΔG⁰, ΔH⁰, ΔS⁰) indicated a spontaneous binding process with negative free energy changes and an entropy driven process due to T∆S0 > ∆H0. A positive value of both enthalpy (ΔH⁰) and entropy (ΔS⁰) changes accompanying the binding showed the driving role of hydrophobic forces in the interaction. Synchronous fluorescence results revealed no considerable changes in the microenvironment of tryptophan (Trp) and tyrosine (Tyr). A visible conformational variation in the secondary structure of HHb especially the α-helix was evident from 3D-fluorescence and circular dichroism (CD) studies. Theoretical docking studies showed the binding site of IVM in the central cavity of HHb. The limitation of this study includes the lack of molecular dynamics simulations to model real-time stability of the complex.

At the 9th World One Health Congress in Lisbon, the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) is calling for a new phase of One Health implementation, prevention and lasting change in countries and communities. A virus moving between wild birds and poultry does not stop to ask which authority is responsible. Antimicrobial resistance does not recognise the boundary between a hospital and a veterinary clinic. Environmental degradation, biodiversity loss and climate change cannot be contained within a single ministry or profession. Yet the systems designed to address these threats often remain divided. Data sit on separate platforms, expertise in different institutions and funding in sector-specific budgets. As experts, policymakers and practitioners gather in Lisbon from 4 to 7 September 2026, the question is no longer whether human, animal and environmental health are interconnected. It is whether our ways of working are evolving quickly enough to reflect that reality. Opening the event, WOAH Director General Dr Emmanuelle Soubeyran called for One Health to move beyond declarations and become a shared practice. At a time when food insecurity, climate change, biodiversity loss and geopolitical instability are converging, One Health is no longer simply an option, but a necessity. However, crossing boundaries does not mean erasing sectoral responsibilities or diluting expertise. Effective collaboration depends on strong Veterinary Services, public health systems, environmental and wildlife institutions, food systems and research capacities, each contributing its expertise to shared goals. “ One Health will not be delivered through declarations alone. It will be delivered in countries, laboratories, hospitals, Veterinary Services, farms and food systems, wildlife and ecosystem management, and, most importantly, in communities ,” Dr Soubeyran said. From global commitments to national action This shift from commitment to implementation is at the centre of WOAH’s participation. The One Health Joint Plan of Action , launched in 2022 by the Quadripartite organisations (FAO, UNEP, WHO and WOAH) provides a common framework for collaboration across human, animal, plant and ecosystem health. But a global framework only becomes meaningful when it changes how institutions work together at national and local levels. How does a country move from endorsing One Health to deciding who is responsible for what? How can ministries share information and accountability? And how can a national plan survive changes in leadership or the end of external funding? These questions will guide “ Bridging Policy-to-Practice: Implementing the One Health Joint Plan of Action at National Level ”, one of WOAH’s priority sessions. Experiences from Uzbekistan, Singapore and Malawi will trace different stages of One Health implementation- from assessing capacities and gaps, bringing the right stakeholders together, to establishing coordination mechanisms and translating priorities into costed national action plans. Evidence from the One Health High-Level Expert Panel (OHHLEP) will highlight the conditions that make implementation last, including political leadership, clear mandates, integrated data, sustainable financing and workforce capacity. The real test of One Health is not whether countries have created a strategy, but whether that strategy changes decisions, budgets and action on the ground. Implementation has to be nationally owned, adequately financed and built into institutions. Otherwise, collaboration risks remaining dependent on individual projects or the urgency of the next crisis. Dr Chadia Wannous, Head of the One Health and Global Frameworks Department at WOAH. A related discussion organised by OHHLEP on translating enablers, dismantling barriers and aligning global policy will explore how to move away from arrangements that appear during emergencies and towards systems capable of working together before a crisis begins. Prevention: connecting science, policy and communities Prevention will be another central theme of WOAH’s contribution. A session co-organised with PREZODE will explore how scientific evidence, policy priorities, local knowledge and lived experience can inform one another and lead to earlier, better decisions. Experiences from Senegal, Viet Nam and global governance will help participants examine recurring obstacles, including short-term financing, weak trust, limited community participation and an “emergency bias” that allows cooperation to fade once the immediate danger has passed. The aim is to create durable interfaces through which knowledge can move in both directions and shape action. Building the systems behind collaboration Plans and structures are only as effective as the people expected to implement them. One Health requires strong technical expertise within each discipline, but also professionals who can understand complex systems, communicate across institutions and build trust with colleagues from other sectors. The FAO/WHO/WOAH Joint One Health Learning Taskforce is working to develop competency-based learning pathways grounded in country and workforce needs. Its session at the Congress will show how existing learning platforms and technical resources can be connected, reducing duplication while combining profession-specific knowledge with skills such as systems thinking, collaboration, communication and leadership. Ministries, universities and training institutions will consider how they can help define, pilot and evaluate future programmes. Effective One Health systems must also recognise that risks are not experienced equally. Social roles influence who interacts with animals, who handles wildlife products, who has access to services and who participates in decisions. A session on gender-transformative approaches will examine how diversity, equity and inclusion can be embedded in governance, financing, data and programmes. WOAH joint work with the International Livestock Research Institute ( ILRI ) on wildmeat value chains offers a concrete example. Hunting is often the most visible activity and may dominate risk assessments. Looking at the entire value chain reveals other roles, including women’s involvement in transporting and selling wildmeat, and forms of exposure that might otherwise remain invisible. Accounting for these realities strengthens both the evidence behind prevention and the policies built from it. From interconnected thinking to connected systems WOAH experts will also contribute to discussions on wildlife health and surveillance, sustainable financing, and the continuing H5N1 panzootic. Though these topics may appear distinct, they lead to the same conclusion: complex threats cannot be addressed through a single intervention or sector. Prevention depends on connecting Veterinary Services, public health authorities, wildlife and environmental institutions, scientists, industry and communities around shared risks. It requires surveillance information to become early warning and action, global frameworks to be adapted to national realities, and political and financial commitment to continue after international attention has moved elsewhere. One Health will ultimately be judged not by the number of strategies produced or meetings held, but by whether countries and communities are better able to prevent threats, protect animals and people, safeguard ecosystems and act together when risks emerge. The challenge now is to turn interconnected thinking into connected systems—and a shared concept into lasting practice. The economic costs from zoonotic and other infectious diseases run into billions of US dollars annually. And according to World Bank estimates, antimicrobial resistance could lead to a loss of around 3.8 percent of global gross domestic product by 2050. These global health threats and potential economic consequences mean that countries need to invest in new ways to increase preparedness and prevention. A new brief from the FAO Investment Centre, in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), examines the long-term, added value of investing in One Health – an integrated approach that recognises the connections between human, animal, plant and ecosystem health. Financial and economic returns to investing in One Health: evidence and future directions looks at how the approach can reduce disease burdens, healthcare costs, environmental contamination and antimicrobial resistance spread. By promoting collaboration across sectors and disciplines, One Health helps maximise the impact of investments while reducing unintended consequences and improving long-term resilience. Geared for decision-makers, One Health practitioners and financing institutions, the brief identifies barriers and opportunities for investing in One Health initiatives and reviews current evidence and knowledge gaps on the returns on investment. It also highlights the institutional and financing mechanisms needed to scale sustainable, cost-effective interventions at all levels, from the community to the global level. Thanawat Tiensin, FAO Assistant Director-General, Director of FAO’s Animal Production and Health Division and Chief Veterinarian, says that “ today’s most pressing challenges – climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, food insecurity and socioeconomic vulnerabilities – are deeply interconnected, ” adding that “ they demand integrated approaches like One Health, which can improve prevention and mitigation .” Baba Soumare, WOAH Deputy Director General, points to animal health as one of the most effective entry points for prevention, adding that: Investing in One Health means investing in stronger Veterinary Services, better surveillance and greater collaboration across sectors to detect, prevent and respond to health threats at their source. These investments protect not only animals, but also people, economies and ecosystems. This investment case is reinforced by WOAH in its 2026 State of the World’s Animal Health report , which warns that infectious animal diseases are becoming more complex and costly while investment in prevention is under increasing pressure. The report highlights that, bringing Veterinary Services worldwide up to international standards would require an investment of approximately US $2.3 billion per year – less than 0.05% of the economic losses of COVID-19 in a single year. Strengthening animal health systems and Veterinary Services is therefore one of the most cost-effective investments countries can make to protect food security, livelihoods, biodiversity and global health, making investment in animal health a cornerstone of effective One Health action. Investments in animal health, food systems, environmental protection and public health can also reinforce one another, delivering greater impact than isolated sectoral interventions. Assistant Director-General and Director of the FAO Investment Centre Mohamed Manssouri says that “ while the wider benefits of investing in One Health are recognised globally, investments in One Health initiatives are still limited. ” He stresses that “ more quantitative evidence of the added value of the One Health approach and support to governments to translate One Health priorities into investment plans are essential for securing continued political commitment as well as investor confidence and engagement .” Dr Jeremy Farrar, Assistant Director-General, WHO, echoes this sentiment, confirming that as “Chair of the Quadripartite, WHO will work with partners to strengthen the evidence on the impact and return on investment of One Health interventions. This is essential to build a stronger scientific and economic case for One Health approach and turn political commitment into action.” This latest brief, part of the FAO Investment Centre’s Innovation and Knowledge for Investment (IK4I) series, adds to FAO’s body of work around One Health. This includes two major studies with the World Bank in Asia and the Pacific, published in 2022, on strengthening investments in livestock health and wildlife systems. Three new reports identify research needs for crustacean, mollusc and amphibian health worldwide WOAH and the STAR IDAZ International Research Consortium (IRC) have published three new reports presenting the outcomes of a global consultation on aquaculture health research, identifying priority areas for crustacean, mollusc and amphibian health. The reports provide guidance for future research investments and international collaboration to strengthen aquatic animal health and support sustainable aquaculture development. Addressing key research gaps in aquatic animal health Aquaculture plays an increasingly important role in global food security, livelihoods and economic development. As the sector faces evolving disease threats, environmental pressures and changing production systems, research and innovation are essential to develop effective solutions for aquatic animal health. Equally important is international research coordination to ensure that limited resources are directed towards the highest-priority needs, promoting collaboration, reducing duplication and accelerating progress towards sustainable and healthy aquaculture systems. To support these efforts, WOAH and the STAR IDAZ International Research Consortium (IRC) have published three new reports presenting the outcomes of the 2025 Global Consultation on Aquaculture Health Research. Focusing on crustaceans, molluscs and amphibians, the reports provide a global assessment of priority research areas identified by experts from around the world. Together with the finfish reports published following the Advancing Aquaculture Health Research workshop held at WOAH Headquarters in Paris in February 2025, these publications contribute to a comprehensive global research agenda for aquatic animal health. Common research priorities: diseases control strategies, diagnostics, vaccines and other antimicrobial alternatives The global consultation was distributed to 440 experts and stakeholders worldwide, including WOAH Aquatic Animal Health Focal Points, WOAH Reference Centres, researchers and other specialists involved in aquatic animal health. Across the three reports, several common priorities emerged. These include improving the understanding and control of high-impact and emerging diseases, developing affordable and field-adapted diagnostic tools, strengthening biosecurity measures and identifying alternatives to antimicrobial use including vaccines. Participants also highlighted the need for greater knowledge of the environmental and climatic factors that influence disease emergence and spread in aquatic production systems. The findings emphasise the importance of developing practical and accessible solutions that can be implemented across diverse production settings and geographical regions. They also highlight opportunities for enhanced international collaboration to address shared challenges and accelerate the development of effective disease prevention and control strategies. Supporting coordinated global action The reports integrate the collaborative discussions on finfish initiated during the WOAH–STAR IDAZ Advancing Aquaculture Health Research workshop and contribute to ongoing efforts to identify knowledge gaps and align research activities at the global level. The findings support the implementation of the WOAH Aquatic Animal Health Strategy and provide valuable guidance for researchers, funding organisations, policy-makers and other stakeholders working to strengthen aquatic animal health and promote sustainable aquaculture development worldwide. Acknowledging global expertise WOAH and STAR IDAZ warmly thank all experts who participated in the consultation and shared their knowledge and experience. Their contributions were essential in developing a globally relevant assessment of aquatic animal health research priorities. WOAH and STAR IDAZ also acknowledge the support of their partners and sponsors, including the International Development Research Centre (IDRC), the Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, the European Commission, DISCONTOOLS, the Norwegian Veterinary Institute (NVI), GALVmed and the Gates Foundation. The reports are available through the WOAH Documentary Portal and the STAR IDAZ Aquatic Diseases Priority Topic webpage. For three decades, WOAH’s official animal health status recognition has supported Members in advancing disease control, facilitating safe trade, and building confidence in Veterinary Services. As the global animal health and trade environment continues to evolve, WOAH is seeking Members’ perspectives on how official status is used in practice and how its value can be further enhanced. WOAH has therefore launched a survey to capture experiences, challenges, and recommendations from Members holding one or more official statuses. Since its introduction in 1996, official status recognition has become one of WOAH’s flagship programmes and a cornerstone of its science-based approach to improving animal health and supporting safe trade. Initially established to officially recognise Members or zones free from foot and mouth disease, the procedure has progressively expanded to include additional diseases, reflecting evolving animal health priorities. As the animal health, trade, and regulatory environment continues to evolve, WOAH is undertaking a review to better understand Members’ experiences and identify opportunities to further strengthen the use, impact and international recognition of official status. Help shape the future of official animal health status recognition To support this effort and as WOAH marks the 30th anniversary of official animal health status recognition, the Organisation has launched a survey targeting Members that hold at least one official animal health status at Member or zonal level. The survey aims to gather insights on Members’ experiences, including the benefits achieved, challenges encountered, and factors that influence the use and recognition of official status, particularly in the context of international trade and risk management. Members’ contributions will help inform recommendations to further enhance the value of official status recognition and strengthen its consistent international acceptance and application. The findings will also support the development of practical options to ensure that the programme continues to meet Members’ needs and remains fit for purpose in a changing global environment. We encourage all eligible Members to participate once they receive the survey invitation. All contributions will help shape the future for WOAH’s official animal health status recognition and ensure that it continues to deliver value to Members and the wider global animal health community. The survey will remain open until 15 September 2026 . The Quadripartite collaboration on One Health – the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) – has agreed to extend the implementation period of the One Health Joint Plan of Action (OH JPA) from 2022–2026 through […] The post Quadripartite collaboration extends the One Health Joint Plan of Action to 2029 appeared first on WOAH - World Organisation for Animal Health . The Quadripartite collaboration on One Health – the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) – has agreed to extend the implementation period of the One Health Joint Plan of Action (OH JPA) from 2022–2026 through to 2029. Ensuring continuity of One Health implementation As the original implementation period was due to conclude in 2026, the extension to 2029 will provide countries with greater predictability for planning, implementing and scaling national One Health priorities under a common global framework. It also enables governments, partners and stakeholders to continue aligning their activities with the extended OH JPA at national, regional and global levels. By maintaining the OH JPA as its shared framework, the Quadripartite will continue to support coordinated, multisectoral collaboration to prevent, detect and respond to health risks at the human, animal, plant and ecosystem interface. Strengthening the Quadripartite collaboration The extension of the OH JPA is also aligned with the renewed Quadripartite Memorandum of Understanding to 2030, which reinforces the long-term collaboration between FAO, UNEP, WHO and WOAH. Together, the renewed MoU and the extended OH JPA provide continuity for the governance and implementation arrangements that guide Quadripartite collaboration on One Health until 2030. They support the continued coordination of technical support to countries, joint advocacy, resource mobilisation efforts and ongoing implementation of One Health at global, regional and national levels. Structured review to inform the next phase of the One Health Joint Plan of Action During the extension period, the Quadripartite organisations will undertake a structured review of the OH JPA to inform the development of its next phase. The review will include: stocktaking of implementation progress at global, regional and national levels; documentation of lessons learned and good practices from implementation across countries and regions; assessment of emerging priorities, evolving One Health needs and the changing global context, including how the framework can continue to respond effectively to evolving One Health priorities; and identification of opportunities to strengthen and refine the OH JPA for future implementation. Looking ahead The extension period will enable the Quadripartite to consolidate progress, respond to emerging One Health priorities, and build a stronger evidence base for the future direction of the OH JPA. Sustained action at country level will also demonstrate how a One Health approach can contribute to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals under the 2030 Agenda. In 2024, wildfires burned approximately 2.6 million hectares of the Pantanal , one of the world’s largest tropical wetlands and one of its richest biodiversity hotspots, destroying habitat for countless wild animals while threatening livestock production and rural livelihoods. The Pantanal is only one example of a growing global challenge. In recent years, severe wildfires have affected Southern Europe, the Amazon Basin, Oceania, parts of North America and many tropical regions, demonstrating that no region is immune. In 2025, an estimated 335 million hectares burned worldwide , illustrating that increasingly severe wildfire seasons are affecting ecosystems, livestock, wildlife and communities across every inhabited continent. As highlighted in the State of the World’s Animal Health 2026 report , the world is facing increasingly complex animal health risks driven by climate change, shifting ecosystems and growing pressure on Veterinary Services. In 2026, El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is further exacerbating drought and extreme weather conditions around the world, increasing the risk and severity of wildfires. Building resilient Veterinary Services is therefore not only an investment in animal health, but also an investment in preparedness for the climate- and environment-related emergencies that are becoming more frequent and more complex. While the devastating impacts of wildfires on people and the environment are widely recognised, their consequences for animals can often receive less attention. Wildfires can cause widespread animal suffering and mortality, disrupt livestock production, destroy habitats and biodiversity, and undermine the livelihoods of rural communities. They can also reshape the way wildlife, farm animals and people interact long after the flames have been extinguished. Displaced wildlife may move into farming areas as well as human settlements, livestock are often relocated across regions, and damaged ecosystems can alter disease dynamics and disease transmission mechanisms. These cascading effects demonstrate why wildfire preparedness requires coordinated action across animal health, public health, environmental and emergency management sectors. Veterinary Services are uniquely positioned to contribute throughout the disaster management cycle. Before wildfires occur, they support prevention (for instance, through promotion of grazing and land use planning), preparedness and emergency planning. During emergencies, they contribute to animal evacuation, emergency veterinary treatment , animal welfare assessments and coordination with emergency responders. In the recovery phase, Veterinary Services help restore essential animal health services, strengthen disease surveillance, monitor the health of livestock and wildlife, and support the recovery of rural livelihoods and affected ecosystems. Protecting animal health and welfare during wildfires also strengthens food security, safeguards biodiversity, supports livelihoods and reinforces community resilience. Integrating Veterinary Services into wildfire preparedness is therefore not only about protecting animals, it is about strengthening the resilience of interconnected human, animal and environmental systems. Despite their critical contribution, Veterinary Services remain insufficiently integrated into national disaster and emergency management systems in many countries. Strengthening their inclusion before, during and after emergencies will help ensure that animal health and welfare are systematically considered as part of disaster risk reduction and response. Across diverse regions, WOAH Members are already demonstrating the value of integrating veterinary expertise into emergency management. In Australia, veterinarians are integrated into emergency animal management through preparedness, response and recovery planning, working alongside emergency authorities to support animal welfare, livestock protection and community resilience during bushfires and other natural disasters. In Brazil, veterinary professionals have played a central role in wildlife rescue , emergency treatment and rehabilitation during the Pantanal wildfires, demonstrating the contribution of veterinary expertise to disaster response in one of the world’s most biodiverse regions. WOAH’s existing international framework provides a strong foundation for this work through its Guidelines on Disaster Management and Risk Reduction in relation to Animal Health and Welfare and Veterinary Public Health , relevant international standards on animal health and welfare, and its commitment to advancing the One Health approach. WOAH also supports Members through training and capacity-building on emergency management using an all-hazards approach, helping strengthen preparedness for a wide range of emergencies, including climate-related disasters. WOAH therefore encourages its Members to: integrate animal health and welfare, including wildlife, into national wildfire preparedness, response and recovery plans; strengthen collaboration between Veterinary Services, emergency management authorities, environmental agencies, wildlife authorities and other relevant partners; invest in resilient Veterinary Services and animal health systems capable of responding effectively to climate- and disaster-related emergencies; adopt a whole-of-society approach that promotes prevention, preparedness and resilient land management, to reduce the impacts of future wildfire emergencies; and promote preparedness measures that protect domestic animals, livestock and wildlife while supporting resilient communities. As wildfire risks continue to grow, protecting animals cannot remain an afterthought. Integrating Veterinary Services into national disaster management systems helps ensure that emergency responses protect not only people, but also the animals, livelihoods and ecosystems that underpin resilient societies. Through its international standards, technical expertise and global network of Members, WOAH remains committed to supporting countries in building resilient Veterinary Services that are equipped to respond to the challenges of a changing world. A major milestone for global health and a strong signal of international commitment to tackling antimicrobial resistance (AMR) : on 21 May 2026, the 183 Members of the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) adopted the updated Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance (GAP-AMR) 2026–2036 during WOAH’s 93rd General Session. The adoption marks a significant achievement for WOAH and the Quadripartite (FAO, UNEP, WHO and WOAH) partnership on AMR, bringing the global community one step closer to a coordinated, One Health response to one of the most pressing challenges facing human, animal, plant and environmental health. Just two days later, Member States of the World Health Organization (WHO) also adopted the updated Plan during the World Health Assembly, reinforcing a shared commitment across sectors and regions to accelerate action against AMR. As the first of the Quadripartite organisations to formally adopt the updated Global Action Plan through its governing body, WOAH demonstrated its leadership and commitment to advancing a coordinated global response to antimicrobial resistance. A roadmap for the next decade The updated GAP-AMR sets out a common vision and strategic direction for the period 2026–2036. It reflects the commitment made by United Nations Member States in the Political Declaration of the High-level Meeting on Antimicrobial Resistance , which called for a robust and inclusive multisectoral response through a One Health approach that aligns with current realities to drive greater impact against antimicrobial resistance. The Plan has six strategic objectives: Strengthen awareness and promote appropriate social and behavioural change Strengthen surveillance systems and laboratory networks to support evidence-based policies and action Intensify infection prevention and control to reduce the burden of infectious diseases and the need for antimicrobials Ensure equitable access, appropriate use and safe disposal of antimicrobials, diagnostics and other health products Accelerate antimicrobial resistance research and innovation Strengthen multisectoral governance, sustainable financing and accountability for a coordinated AMR response By addressing AMR through a One Health approach, the Plan recognises the interconnectedness of human, animal, plant and environmental health and the need for collective action to preserve the effectiveness of antimicrobials for future generations. Adoption by WOAH Members The updated Global Action Plan was adopted by WOAH Members through Resolution No. 18 , submitted to the 2026 World Assembly of Delegates following the recommendation of the WOAH Working Group on Antimicrobial Resistance. The adoption reflects the intensive collaboration among the Quadripartite organisations, Member Delegations, technical experts, partner organisations and stakeholders across sectors who contributed to the development of the updated GAP-AMR through extensive consultations. From strategy to implementation The adoption of the updated GAP-AMR is not the end of the process – it is the beginning of a new phase focused on implementation. While the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) continue their respective approval processes, the Quadripartite partners are already preparing the next steps. A key priority will be the development of cross-sectoral operational guidance to support Members of the Quadripartite organisations and regions in translating the strategic objectives of the GAP-AMR into practical action. These guidelines will provide a framework for coordinated implementation across sectors and will help strengthen accountability, monitoring and impact. Furthermore, the Quadripartite is also developing a Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) Framework that will allow to assess the progress in the implementation of the updated GAP-AMR at global level. WOAH is also preparing a series of webinars to support Members in advancing AMR action within Veterinary Services and animal health systems. A collective achievement The adoption of the updated Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance represents the power of international cooperation and collective action. It is the result of sustained engagement from governments, experts, international organisations and non-state actors committed to protecting the effectiveness of antimicrobials and safeguarding health worldwide. As the global community moves from commitment to implementation, WOAH remains fully committed to supporting its Members and partners in delivering meaningful action against antimicrobial resistance. The next decade will be decisive. The roadmap is now in place; the focus turns to putting the Plan into practice. Participants were randomized to a 16-week moderate-intensity AE plus nutritional consultation (AE group; n = 25) or nutritional consultation alone (control group, CG; n = 25). RESULTS: Of the 50 participants (mean age, 62.6 ± 7.0 years; 60% female), 44 participants completed the study. Although most outcomes showed no statistically significant between-group differences, LMM analysis confirmed a significant reduction in the low-frequency to high-frequency (LF/HF) (β = -0.87, p = 0.04), indicating worsening ANS while AE remained stable. A 78-Year-Old Man With a Previously Stable Atherosclerotic Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Presenting With Impending Rupture Following COVID-19.
BACKGROUND Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) rupture is a life-threatening condition. Although elective repair is generally guided by aneurysm size, impending rupture can occur when rapid aneurysmal expansion or periaortic inflammatory changes develop before overt hemodynamic deterioration. This report describes the case of a 78-year-old man with a previously stable 43-mm atherosclerotic AAA who presented with impending rupture after coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). CASE REPORT A 78-year-old Japanese man with a known AAA under imaging surveillance developed fever and was diagnosed with COVID-19 by nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction testing. Seven days later, he was admitted for recurrent fever, cough, poor appetite, and elevated inflammatory markers. His medical history included hypertension, heavy smoking, advanced chronic kidney disease, and diffuse atherosclerotic disease. The aneurysm had shown minimal growth over 2 years, with a stable maximum short-axis diameter of approximately 43 mm on serial computed tomography. After admission, C-reactive protein levels initially decreased but rose again on hospital day 11, accompanied by new-onset mild low back pain and no marked blood pressure elevation or hemodynamic instability. Repeat non-contrast abdominal computed tomography performed 18 days after COVID-19 diagnosis demonstrated rapid AAA expansion from 43 mm to 51 mm within 2 months, with periaortic fat stranding, consistent with impending rupture. Urgent endovascular aneurysm repair was performed before hemodynamic deterioration. The postoperative course was stable, and the patient was discharged without ischemic or procedural complications. CONCLUSIONS This case shows that a previously stable AAA can abruptly destabilize after recent COVID-19. Repeat imaging should be considered when inflammatory markers rise or new symptoms occur, even when symptoms are mild.

Hypervirulent Listeria isolated from a wild rabbit in Canada.
Listeria monocytogenes is the causative agent of listeriosis, a major foodborne disease with a 30% mortality rate in humans. Although L. monocytogenes can infect animals, whether wildlife can serve as a reservoir remains understudied, especially in Canada. [Postgraduate training in anesthesiology in Germany : Challenges and perspectives].
INTRODUCTION: Postgraduate medical training in anesthesiology in Germany faces a variety of challenges, including high competency requirements, staffing shortages, the implementation of competence-based training programs and the potential long-term effects of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) pandemic. METHODS: This secondary analysis focuses on the German subgroup of a survey conducted by the European Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care (ESAIC), as reported by Dow et al. Using descriptive statistics, the study analyzed training conditions, supervision, workload, pandemic-related impacts on training and the consideration of work abroad and examined these factors within a European context. RESULTS: A total of 140 doctors in training from Germany completed the questionnaire. Although the results largely align with European trends, only a comparatively small proportion of respondents (38%) reported receiving adequate supervision. With a median of 50 working hours per week and regular overtime, the workload is high and 37% reported considering working abroad. Whilst the majority reported no significant pandemic-related disruption to their training, a substantial minority reported restrictions on acquiring practical skills or a lack of opportunities to catch up on missed content. DISCUSSION: The findings underscore the need for improved supervision, competence-based training concepts, and adequate staffing. Coordinated measures by all relevant stakeholders, from hospital management to professional societies, appear necessary to improve the training and working conditions associated with the consideration of working abroad.

Unexpected coagulopathy in thrombolyzed stroke: experience from a single center in Chile.
BACKGROUND: The effectiveness of intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) for acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is time-dependent, and waiting for coagulation tests (COT) may delay treatment initiation. In several countries, IVT is initiated without waiting COT results; this approach has not been evaluated in South America. In this region, excessive alcohol consumption may increase the prevalence of unrecognized chronic liver disease. OBJECTIVE: To determine the frequency of unsuspected coagulation abnormalities among patients with AIS treated with IVT at a single tertiary care center in Chile. METHODS: A prospective analysis of all patients treated with IVT at Clínica Alemana between June 2016 and July 2025, assessing the proportion of individuals with unexpected coagulation abnormalities. RESULTS: A total of 480 patients with AIS received IVT. The COTs were normal in 445 patients (92.7%), abnormal in 9 (1.88%), and incomplete or not performed in 26 (5.42%). No clinical differences were observed among the three groups. Patients with coagulation abnormalities or incomplete/not performed COT were significantly less frequent in the Emergency Room (ER) during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (p = 0.001). Among those with abnormal COT results, significant differences were found in international normalized ratio (INR) values (p < 0.000) and platelet count (p = 0.001). The functional outcomes at 3 months, as well as mortality and rate of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage, did not differ across groups. CONCLUSION: Unexpected coagulation disorders are an infrequent finding in patients with AIS treated with IVT at our center in Santiago, Chile. Therefore, blood test results should not be awaited before initiating IVT.

Antibiotic overuse and mortality in patients hospitalised for COVID-19: a global cohort study.
BACKGROUND: Global antibiotic use during the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact remain unclear. This study analysed antibiotic use, bacterial co-infections, and the association between antibiotic use and in-hospital mortality among patients hospitalised for COVID-19, using a WHO database. METHODS: We conducted a multicountry cohort study using anonymised patient-level data from The WHO Global Clinical Platform for COVID-19. Data were collected across 64 countries in all six WHO regions between January, 2020, and October, 2023. The study included hospitalised patients of all ages with suspected or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. We obtained patient-level data from standardised WHO case report forms completed prospectively or retrospectively and from harmonised national registries, research studies, and hospital databases. Patients without a suspected or confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis or missing information on hospital admission date, antibiotic use, or outcome were excluded from the analysis. Patients were followed up from hospital admission until death, discharge, transfer, or 28 days, whichever occurred first. Follow-up data were collected at hospital discharge or death by the treating facility and entered into the platform. The primary outcome was 28-day in-hospital mortality, and we analysed this outcome using Cox proportional hazards models with a shared frailty term to account for country-level clustering. FINDINGS: The median age of the study population was 61·9 years (±21·7), with 198 223 women and 251 990 men with data available on antibiotic use. Of the 592 898 patients enrolled, 451 291 (76·1%) had data on antibiotic use and were included in the descriptive analysis; 122 854 had complete data on empirical treatment type, of whom 47 359 (38·5%) were included in the regression analysis. Among the 451 291 patients with data on antibiotic use, 341 125 (75·6%) received antibiotics, more frequently in severe to critical cases than in mild to moderate cases (80·5% vs 71·6%). Prescribing was highest in the Eastern Mediterranean (83·0%) and African (82·7%) regions and lowest in the Western Pacific region (32·8%), declining in the European region and region of the Americas but increasing in the African region between 2020 and 2022. Treatment was predominantly empirical and involved Watch antibiotics of the WHO Access, Watch, and Reserve classification. Clinically suspected co-infections were reported in 47 050 (7·9%) of the 592 898 patients; among those with positive cultures, 1815 (42·8%) of 4237 had multidrug-resistant bacteria. In the unadjusted analyses, empirical antibiotic use was associated with higher mortality across severity strata. After adjustment for age, sex, comorbidities, and disease severity, empirical antibiotic use remained associated with increased mortality in mild to moderate cases (adjusted hazard ratio 1·80, 95% CI 1·36-2·38) and severe to critical cases (1·16, 1·08-1·24). INTERPRETATION: Despite clinically suspected co-infections being reported in only 47 050 (7·9%) of the 592 898 enrolled patients, 341 125 (75·6%) of the 451 291 patients with data on antibiotic use received antibiotic therapy, predominantly broad-spectrum agents. As antibiotic use was not associated with improved clinical outcomes and is known to increase antimicrobial resistance, it should be rationalised through strengthened antimicrobial stewardship and behavioural interventions, particularly during respiratory viral epidemics. FUNDING: None.

Online continuing education for the Indian Health Service: Public health intervention wheel update.
BACKGROUND: Following the work-priority disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the supervisor of the Four Corners Regional Health Center of the Indian Health Service requested an update of the Public Health Intervention Wheel for public health staff across 11 healthcare facilities. The Wheel explains what public health nurses do in their practice. PURPOSE: Nursing leaders chose a staff development project to help public health nursing staff shift their focus to address health priorities and health disparities among Native American communities. METHODS: Public health nursing staff completed five synchronous online sessions on the revised Public Health Intervention Wheel. The online sessions included PowerPoint presentations, discussion, and group reports. Participants reported that the Public Health Intervention Wheel applied to and explained their practice. A survey revealed that 93% to 97% of participants strongly agreed or agreed that the learning objectives were met and the learning strategies were effective. DISCUSSION: The online education format provided convenient access for participants over a large geographic area. Both the benefits and challenges of the online synchronous education sessions were identified. CONCLUSION: The integration of the Wheel into staff orientation and departmental initiatives will contribute to a comprehensive scope of public health nursing practice in Native American communities.

Experimental assessment of medical plastic waste pyrolysis and steam gasification for resource recovery.
Medical plastic waste (MPW) has become a major environmental concern due to its massive production in clinics and hospitals, and the limited recycling options, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic. In this context, thermochemical technologies represent a promising approach to simultaneously reduce and valorize this waste by producing three main streams of value: a gaseous, a liquid, and a solid stream. In this study, the thermochemical conversion of four representative categories of MPW (non-woven medical textiles, FFP2 face masks, Pasteur pipettes, and natural latex gloves) was experimentally evaluated under different operating conditions. The experiments were conducted in a laboratory-scale fluidized-bed reactor at temperatures between 750 and 850°C using N2 at 8 NL min-1 or N2 plus steam (6 NL min-1N2 + 2 NL min-1 steam) as the process atmosphere, in order to compare predominantly pyrolytic and steam gasification conditions. These conditions correspond to nominal freeboard residence times of approximately 2.4-2.6 s. The results revealed a strong influence of both feedstock composition and operating conditions. The gas composition varied significantly with the type of MPW, leading to H2 and CO contents reaching up to 30 vol% and 20 vol%, respectively, both for FFP2 face masks under N2 and at 750°C. Carbon conversion to the gas phase achieved a maximum of approximately 45%. Steam addition significantly reduced carbon retention in the char fraction, while the unaccounted carbon fraction remained substantial under several steam gasification conditions. Tar analysis showed that benzene, toluene and xylene (BTX) compounds predominated for polypropylene- and polyethylene- based MPW, whereas natural latex gloves exhibited a greater tendency towards the formation of substituted aromatic compounds, naphthalene derivatives and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of thermochemical conversion to recover valuable products from selected MPW fractions and provide an experimental basis for identifying suitable feedstock-specific operating conditions. Further development towards industrial implementation will require consideration of process efficiency and environmental performance.

Ischemic stroke after bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination and influenza vaccination during the 2022-2023 season: a multi-site self-controlled case series study.
BACKGROUND: The Vaccine Safety Datalink (VSD) detected a statistical signal for ischemic events (ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack) following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination through prospective surveillance during 2022-2023. Although multiple studies from other surveillance systems and countries reported no increased risk, important methodological limitations remained. This U.S. study addressed those limitations by evaluating the ischemic stroke risk following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, influenza vaccination, and their same-day coadministration using an event-dependent self-controlled case series (SCCS) design. METHODS: Study outcomes included first-ever ischemic stroke (primary outcome), first-in-1-year ischemic stroke (secondary outcome), and ischemic events (exploratory outcomes), identified using ICD-10-CM codes in inpatient and emergency department settings during September 1, 2022-March 31, 2023, among individuals aged ≥12 years across eight VSD sites. Analyses were conducted separately for Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna bivalent vaccines, with relative incidences (RI) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) estimated for 1-21-day and 1-42-day risk intervals, using person-time outside these intervals as the control period. Subgroup analyses were performed by age group (12-64, ≥65 years) and history of documented SARS-CoV-2 infection. RESULTS: A total of 6510 first-ever ischemic strokes were identified among more than 6.8 million participants. Among recipients of Pfizer-BioNTech bivalent COVID-19 and influenza vaccines, no statistically significant increased risk of first-ever ischemic stroke was observed following bivalent COVID-19 vaccination (RI = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.63-1.41), influenza vaccination (RI = 0.95; 95% CI: 0.82-1.10), or same-day coadministration (RI = 1.15; 95% CI: 0.88-1.49) within 1-21-day risk intervals; findings were similar for 1-42-day intervals. Comparable null results were observed for Moderna vaccine and across all subgroups, secondary, and exploratory outcomes. CONCLUSION: No increased risk of ischemic stroke was found following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, influenza vaccination, or their coadministration in this multi-site SCCS study. These findings are consistent with previous studies and underscore the importance of continued vaccine safety monitoring.

Content and Quality Analysis of Chikungunya Fever-Related Online Information on Social Media: A Cross-Sectional Study.
An outbreak of chikungunya fever (CHIKF) occurred in China in 2025. The rapid increase in new cases has drawn the attention of health authorities.
