MAIN CONCLUSIONS: Given its potential role as a vector of chikungunya, dengue, Zika and yellow fever, continued entomological surveillance and early detection in the Caribbean and the Americas are needed.

Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic?
Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness.

Recovery of Human Pegiviruses from Patients with Acute Febrile Illness and Sub-acute Central Nervous System Infection.
OBJECTIVE: To describe two cases of HPgV-1 identified during high-throughput sequencing (HTS)-based investigation of previously undiagnosed acute febrile illness (AFI) and central nervous system infection. METHODS: RNA metagenomic HTS was applied to clinical samples that had previously tested negative by PCR targeting alphaviruses, flaviviruses, enteroviruses, herpesviruses, and paramyxoviruses. Specimens were also tested for IgM antibodies against chikungunya virus, dengue virus, and Japanese encephalitis virus. RESULTS: A complete HPgV-1 genotype 4 was recovered from a child with undifferentiated AFI. In a middle-aged man with HIV and severe neurological disorder, complete genomes of HPgV-1 (genotype 4), HPgV-2, and hepatitis C virus (genotype 3k) were identified. CONCLUSION: To our knowledge, this is the first report of HPgV-2 detection in Indonesia, expanding its known geographic distribution. These findings underscore the complexity of viral co-infections in immunocompromised patients and the uncertain clinical significance of human pegiviruses. This further highlights the utility of metagenomic HTS for pathogen discovery and genomic surveillance in unexplained clinical syndromes.

Oropouche virus infection in pregnant women in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil: a prospective cohort study.
BACKGROUND: Although adverse maternal and infant outcomes have been reported following Oropouche virus infection, the frequencies of these outcomes have not been compared with those in uninfected pregnancies. We followed up pregnant women from areas with Oropouche virus transmission in Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, to evaluate potential adverse maternal and infant outcomes following Oropouche virus exposure. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study across the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, we included pregnant women receiving prenatal care in municipalities with or at high risk of Oropouche virus outbreaks. Inclusion criteria were: ongoing risk of Oropouche virus infection at the time of prenatal visit; prenatal care at one of the participating sites; and willingness and ability to consent to and participate in the study. Exclusion criteria included infection with other arboviruses and fetal chromosomal abnormalities. Maternal blood, urine, and saliva were collected and tested for Oropouche virus by RT-PCR at enrolment and pregnancy endpoints. IgG and IgM serologies from maternal blood, placental tissue PCR, and immunohistochemistry were done. Confirmed infections were defined by: positive Oropouche virus PCR in blood, urine, saliva, or placenta; positive Oropouche virus placental immunohistochemistry; or Oropouche virus-specific IgM or IgG seroconversion. Possible infection was defined as one positive IgM result without a positive PCR. Negative results ruled out infection. Adverse maternal outcomes (reported by study investigators following up participants at study sites) were maternal death or disability, fetal loss, or haemorrhage; adverse infant outcomes were neonatal death or malformations. Relative risks adjusted for maternal age, other congenital infections, and use of tobacco, alcohol, and drugs during pregnancy for adverse maternal and infant outcomes were calculated. FINDINGS: Between Nov 29, 2024, and Oct 8, 2025, 544 participants were enrolled: 130 (24%) with confirmed, 143 (26%) with possible, and 271 (50%) with no Oropouche virus infection. The median cycle threshold value of RT-PCR was 29·7 (IQR 25·8-34·9). Among the 130 women with confirmed infection, 104 (80%) developed detectable IgG antibodies. Symptoms were present in 80 (62%) women with confirmed infection, not necessarily associated with adverse outcomes (adjusted relative risk [aRR] 0∙84 [95% credible interval 0∙51-1∙21]). By the end of follow-up, the pregnancies of 119 women with confirmed infection and 193 with no infection had resulted in livebirth, stillbirth, or miscarriage; 105 (88%) women with confirmed infection had livebirths and 187 (97%) women without infection had livebirths. Adverse maternal outcomes occurred in 21 (18%) women with confirmed infection and 14 (7%) women with no infection (aRR 2∙90 [1∙52-5∙35]). Fetal loss and haemorrhage risk were three times higher in women with confirmed infection than in those with no infection (aRR 3∙08 [1∙28-7∙29] for fetal loss and 2∙79 [1∙22-6∙21] for haemorrhage). The aRR for adverse infant outcomes was 9∙18 (1∙89-47∙88). CNS abnormalities occurred in eight (8%) infants of mothers with confirmed infection and in no infants of mothers with no infection. INTERPRETATION: Oropouche virus infection during pregnancy is associated with severe maternal and infant outcomes, including maternal haemorrhage, fetal loss, and infant CNS abnormalities. FUNDING: The Carlos Chagas Filho Foundation for Research Support of the State of Rio de Janeiro (FAPERJ), the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development (CNPq), the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (Fiocruz), and the European Health and Digital Executive Agency. TRANSLATION: For the Portuguese translation of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

Incidence and aetiology of diarrhoeal disease among children under five years in the post-rotavirus vaccine introduction era in Manhiça District, Mozambique.
BACKGROUND: Diarrhoea remains a major cause of death in children under five, despite the global decline in hospitalisations following the widespread introduction of rotavirus vaccines . As rotavirus-associated disease declines, it is important to identify other diarrhoea associated pathogens, although post-vaccine data remain limited in Mozambique. This study aimed to estimate the incidence and determine the aetiology of Moderate-to-Severe Diarrhoea (MSD) and Less Severe Diarrhoea (LSD) among children under five, post-rotavirus vaccine introduction in Manhiça District, a rural setting in Mozambique. METHODS: We estimated the incidence of diarrhoea using data from the morbidity surveillance and pathogen-attributable fractions based on analysis of stool specimens collected in a case-control study. RESULTS: The overall incidence of MSD was 5.6 cases per 1,000 child-years at risk (CYAR), with the highest rate observed among infants aged 0-11 months (15.5 per 1,000 CYAR) with a declining trend over time. LSD incidence was approximately 20 times higher than MSD incidence (119.7 per 1,000 CYAR), peaking among children aged 12-23 months (232.9 per 1,000 CYAR). Rotavirus remained the leading cause of both MSD and LSD among infants aged 0-11 months, while other important pathogens associated with LSD in this age group included sapovirus and Cryptosporidium spp. Among children aged 12-23 months, enteroaggregative Escherichia coli and adenovirus 40/41 were the major contributors to MSD. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight that rotavirus remains an important diarrhoea aetiology among infants and demonstrate changes on diarrhoea aetiologies post-rotavirus vaccine introduction; reinforcing the need for continued surveillance to better inform control and prevention strategies.

Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in Black-Horned Capuchin Monkeys, Brazil.
We carried out a viral surveillance study on 30 black-horned capuchin monkeys (Sapajus nigritus) in Rio Doce State Park, a protected area in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Samples were tested for orthopoxviruses, flaviviruses, coronaviruses, influenza viruses, and a wide range of other respiratory viruses using molecular and serological methods. RT-qPCR detected the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) genome in oral swabs from two asymptomatic juvenile females sampled in an area with high human interaction. This finding indicates a possible exposure of an population to RSV, a contagious human pathogen, and highlights the importance of increased surveillance at the human-wildlife interface.

Genomic surveillance of an imported recombinant Clade Ib and IIb monkeypox virus case in India.
Double-stranded DNA viruses can recombine, such as the monkeypox virus (MPXV), but only one recombinant MPXV has been reported previously in the UK. Here we characterize a recombinant Clade Ib and IIb MPXV isolated from a travel-associated mpox case in India. The mosaic genome contains clade-defining mutations from both Ib and IIb and clusters with the UK recombinant. Both recombinant viruses show 34 recombinant tracts and 21 recombinant lineage-associated mutations. This has implications for genomic surveillance and diagnostics.

Public Health Impact of Adjuvanted RSVPreF3 Vaccination Among US Adults Aged ≥60 Years Residing in Long-Term Care Settings.
OBJECTIVES: Adults aged ≥60 years and adults with certain health conditions are at increased risk for severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease, which can have a substantial clinical burden. Residents in long-term care settings often have multiple risk factors, including age ≥60 years, underlying health conditions, and/or frailty, compounding risk for severe RSV disease. This study evaluated the public health impact of adjuvanted RSV prefusion F3 (RSVPreF3) vaccination on averted RSV disease burden. DESIGN: Public health impact analysis using a static, multicohort Markov model. SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS: United States (US) adults aged ≥60 years residing in long-term care settings. METHODS: Adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccination vs no vaccination was simulated over 5 years using real-world RSV vaccination uptake data. Other model inputs have been previously validated and reported. This analysis estimated avoided RSV-related health outcomes due to vaccination, as well as the number needed to vaccinate (NNV) to avoid RSV-related outcomes. RESULTS: Among the modeled 2,113,600 US adults aged ≥60 years residing in long-term care settings, 378,656 were simulated to receive 1 dose of adjuvanted RSVPreF3. RSV vaccination resulted in 33,989 fewer RSV cases, including 7688 fewer RSV-upper respiratory tract disease cases and 26,302 fewer RSV-lower respiratory tract disease cases (RSV-LRTD). Avoided healthcare resource use included 19,639 fewer outpatient visits, 1556 fewer emergency department visits, and 11,634 fewer hospitalizations. RSV-related deaths declined by 1355 over 5 years, alongside 7221 and 6043 fewer discounted life years and quality-adjusted life years lost, respectively. To avoid 1 RSV-LRTD case, the estimated NNV was 14 individuals. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: Adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccination avoided a substantial number of negative health outcomes among US adults aged ≥60 years residing in long-term care settings, providing evidence of its impact as a prevention strategy. Future efforts are needed to ensure that long-term care residents have access to RSV vaccination.

Prolonged low-level inter-human mpox transmission in Nigeria prior to the global outbreak in 2022: a mathematical modelling study.
BACKGROUND: The 2022 global mpox outbreak was linked to clade IIb viruses that previously circulated in Nigeria. Genomic evidence suggests that, in Nigeria, sustained human-to-human transmission may have begun as early as 2016. METHODS: Using a stochastic branching process model, we investigated the conditions under which mpox could have persisted at low levels in Nigeria between 2016 and April 2022 without triggering a clearly recognized outbreak and quantified the potential hidden burden of infection and international exportation. RESULTS: We found that when R is close to 1 and secondary infections show low variability (low heterogeneity, i.e. no superspreading), sustained but slow transmission can persist with non-negligible probability. Under our baseline modelling assumptions (R = 1.0, Poisson offspring distribution), 9% of simulations resulted in cryptic epidemics that lasted throughout the study period. Conditional on a trajectory being classified as cryptic under this scenario, the average epidemic size was 8,500 infections (95% prediction interval: 2,900-17,000) per cryptic epidemic, compared with 241 confirmed cases reported. This implies substantial under ascertainment with a detection rate of 2.8% (95% prediction interval: 1.4-8.3%). Estimated exportations to Europe and North America were consistent with the small number of documented travel-associated cases before 2022. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the plausibility of prolonged, low-level mpox transmission in Nigeria prior to the recognized global outbreak.

Prevalence of respiratory viruses among pilgrims in Saudi Arabia during the Hajj 2026: a cross-sectional study.
BACKGROUND: Hajj is one of the world's largest annual mass gatherings and provides favorable conditions for respiratory virus transmission because of intense crowding and extensive international travel. Contemporary post-pandemic molecular surveillance data remain limited. This study investigated the prevalence, determinants, and characteristics of respiratory virus detections among pilgrims during the 2026 Hajj season. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among adult domestic and international pilgrims over an extended peri-Hajj period (before, during and after Hajj) in the year 2026. Participants completed a structured questionnaire and provided combined nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swab specimens for multiplex real-time RT-PCR detection of common respiratory viruses. A subset of positive samples underwent genomic sequencing for viral subtype and variant characterization. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with laboratory-confirmed respiratory viral infection. RESULTS: Among 412 enrolled pilgrims across all three phases, 58 (14.1%) tested positive for at least one respiratory virus. The prevalence of viral detection was 6.7% pre-Hajj, 16.0% during Hajj and 21.4% post-Hajj. Influenza A was the predominant virus (34.5%), followed by rhinovirus (24.1%), SARS-CoV-2 (20.7%), respiratory syncytial virus (13.8%), adenovirus (5.2%), and seasonal human coronaviruses (1.7%). Diabetes mellitus, chronic lung disease and smoking were independently associated with increased odds of respiratory virus detection. Conversely, receipt of pre-travel health advice, influenza vaccination and regular facemask use were independently associated with reduced odds of respiratory virus detection. CONCLUSIONS: Respiratory virus transmission remains an important public health concern during Hajj. Strengthening pre-travel health advice, promoting influenza vaccination, and reinforcing personal preventive measures may reduce respiratory viral transmission during Hajj and other international mass gatherings.

Cost‑effectiveness analysis of the mRNA‑1345 RSV vaccine for older adults in Italy.
AIMS: To evaluate the potential public health impact and cost-effectiveness of vaccination using mRNA-1345 administered as a single dose compared with no vaccination in Italian high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years. METHODS: A static decision-analytic model was developed to project clinical and economic outcomes over a five-year time horizon, assuming 50% vaccination coverage among eligible adults. Economic outcomes were evaluated from the Italian National Health Service (Servizio Sanitario Nazionale, SSN) perspective. Model inputs were informed by the most recent Italian epidemiological, clinical, and economic evidence, supplemented by published international data when necessary. Deterministic, probabilistic, and scenario analyses were conducted to assess the impact of uncertainty in model inputs and assumptions on the study results. RESULTS: Vaccination with mRNA-1345 in high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥75 years was projected to avert over 19,800 hospitalizations, 4,000 emergency department visits, 381,000 outpatient visits, 6,000 RSV-attributable deaths, and 212,000 antibiotic prescriptions compared with no vaccination over a five-year period. The total incremental cost of €1,143 million and the additional 47,477 QALYs gained resulted in an ICER of €24,078 per QALY gained, which was below the commonly referenced willingness-to-pay range of €33,000-40,000/QALY. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness of the analysis results. LIMITATIONS: Due to limited epidemiological evidence for Italy, selected epidemiological inputs were informed by studies conducted in other high-income countries. In addition, vaccine efficacy beyond the two-year clinical trial follow-up was projected to five years using nonlinear waning curves fitted to the observed trial data. CONCLUSIONS: Vaccination with mRNA-1345 is a cost-effective strategy for the prevention of RSV in high-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults ≥75 years in Italy, in comparison to no vaccination, and has the potential to provide substantial public health benefits.

Pandemic-Responsive Molecularly Imprinted Polymer-Based Electrochemical Sensor for Mpox Detection.
In 2022, a global Mpox outbreak occurred, and the World Health Organization (WHO) declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC). Although the outbreak was quickly constrained, new cases of infection associated with mutated virions continue to be documented worldwide. In recent global health crises, there is an urgent need to develop rapid, cost-effective diagnostic assays. While nucleic acid assays (e.g., PCR and CRISPR-based methods) represent the current gold standard for Mpox virus (MPXV) detection, point-of-care (POC) assays for Mpox remain limited. Here, we developed a molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP)-based MPXV sensor targeting A29L, a surface protein involved in host cell binding. The MIP sensor exhibits a remarkable detection limit of 7.7 pg/mL (0.54 pM). Moreover, we demonstrated that the MIP sensor detected A29L in artificial interstitial fluid (AIF) with a detection limit of 12.4 pg/mL (0.86 pM), supporting sensitive detection in a lesion-relevant model matrix. The MIP sensor preferentially responded to A29L over MPXV B6R, vaccinia virus A27L, and biointerferents and retained its response after 30 days. The results indicate that the MIP-based MPXV sensor has strong potential for clinical Mpox detection and could serve as a valuable diagnostic platform in future pandemics.

Exploiting key metabolic pathways of Mycobacterium tuberculosis for next-generation anti-tubercular drug discovery.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) caused disease Tuberculosis (TB) continues to be one of the leading causes of mortality although decades of medical research has progressed. With the alarming rise in multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains, the effectiveness of conventional therapeutic regimens is being severely compromised. This mounting resistance not only diminishes the clinical success of existing drugs but also poses a significant health threat, underscoring the urgent need to develop innovative therapeutic strategies that can overcome resistance mechanisms and restore treatment efficacy. Recent research has revealed that Mtb relies on unique metabolic adaptations for its survival and persistence within the host, particularly through the shikimate pathway, the methylcitrate cycle and the glyoxylate shunt. These pathways enable the bacterium to synthesize essential metabolites, detoxify toxic intermediates and conserve carbon skeletons under nutrient deficient conditions. The enzymes involved in these pathways exhibit distinct structural and functional features that are absent in humans, making them highly selective as drug targets. Advances in structural biology, enzyme kinetics and computational approaches have facilitated the discovery of promising inhibitors derived from natural products, synthetic scaffolds and fragment-based designs. This review discusses the mechanistic insights, regulatory roles and inhibitor development efforts targeting key enzymes from these three metabolic pathways. By integrating biochemical, structural and medicinal chemistry perspectives, here in the potential of these metabolic nodes as underexploited yet powerful avenues for next-generation anti-tubercular drug discovery are reviewed.

In Silico Design and Immunogenicity Evaluation of a Multiepitope Vaccine Candidate Against Leishmania tropica in BALB/c Mice.
BACKGROUND: Cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania tropica remains a major neglected parasitic disease with limited therapeutic options and frequent treatment failure, highlighting the urgent need for effective vaccine-based interventions. Multiepitope vaccine (MEV) strategies provide a rational and targeted approach to induce defined cellular and humoral immune responses against Leishmania infection. METHODS: In this study, a MEV candidate was designed using conserved cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), helper T lymphocyte (HTL), and linear B-cell epitopes derived from immunodominant Leishmania antigens. Prior to experimental evaluation, protein-protein docking was performed to assess the interaction between the vaccine candidate and the TLR4 receptor. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were subsequently conducted using NAMD 3.0.0 with the CHARMM36 force field under physiological conditions (TIP3P water model, 0.15 M NaCl, pH 7.4). Structural parameters including root mean square deviation (RMSD), radius of gyration (Rg), and principal component analysis (PCA) were calculated. The recombinant construct was expressed in an Escherichia coli pET-20b (+) system and purified using affinity chromatography. The vaccine was evaluated in a BALB/c mouse model using a multidose subcutaneous immunization protocol followed by L. tropica challenge. Immunological responses were assessed by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of cytokine gene expression (IL-12, IFN-γ, and IL-4) and by Western blot analysis for detection of antigen-specific antibodies. Safety was evaluated based on survival and observation of apparent adverse effects during the experimental period. RESULTS: Computational analysis demonstrated stable interaction between the vaccine candidate and the TLR4 receptor. MD simulations confirmed the formation of a stable and compact vaccine-TLR4 complex, supported by RMSD, Rg, and PCA analyses, indicating reduced conformational fluctuations and enhanced receptor stabilization compared with the unbound state. Immunological analysis revealed a strong Th1-skewed immune response characterized by significant upregulation of IFN-γ, modulation of IL-12 expression, and marked downregulation of IL-4 following challenge. Western blot analysis confirmed specific antigen recognition in vaccinated mice, whereas control groups showed no detectable reactivity. No mortality, behavioral changes, or apparent vaccine-related adverse effects were observed during the observation period, supporting the tolerability of the vaccine under the experimental conditions. CONCLUSION: Overall, the MEV induced coordinated cellular immune responses together with antigen-specific antibody recognition. The observed cytokine gene expression profile and antibody reactivity indicate a robust immunogenic response and support the recombinant construct as a promising candidate for further preclinical evaluation against cutaneous leishmaniasis. Additional studies assessing protective efficacy, parasite burden, and long-term immune durability are warranted.

Nucleic acid technologies in crustacean disease management: Diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance.
Crustacean aquaculture, particularly shrimp, crab, and lobster production, contributes around US$10 billion annually to the global food supply but remains highly vulnerable to viral and bacterial diseases. Pathogens such as White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV), Yellow Head Virus (YHV), Taura Syndrome Virus (TSV), and Vibrio species continue to cause substantial economic losses, and conventional management based on visual inspection, histopathology, and antimicrobial treatment is often slow and insensitive. This review examines how nucleic acid technologies are reshaping diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance in crustacean health management. Molecular diagnostic platforms including PCR, quantitative PCR, reverse transcription PCR, loop mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, and multiplex assays allow rapid, sensitive, and specific detection of pathogens, often before clinical signs appear. RNA interference shows strong therapeutic promise against viral pathogens, with experimental studies reporting 40 to 80% reductions in cumulative mortality, although stability, dosing, delivery, and production cost continue to limit commercial use. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) and Cas (CRISPR-associated) has emerged as a powerful platform for functional genomics, immune gene characterisation, and the future development of disease resistant strains, though application in crustaceans remains largely proof of concept. Environmental DNA and molecular biosurveillance enable early pathogen detection through water and sediment sampling, supporting proactive biosecurity and precision aquaculture. Persistent barriers include scalability, infrastructure gaps in producing regions, regulatory uncertainty, and public acceptance. Future progress will rely on improved delivery systems, expanded crustacean genomic resources, and integration of molecular tools with digital farm management to deliver sustainable disease control.

Infectious African Swine Fever Virus in Spray-Dried Porcine Plasma Used as Feed Ingredient, South Korea, 2026.
We detected African swine fever virus DNA in feed and spray-dried porcine plasma (SDPP) used as a feed ingredient in South Korea. Pigs inoculated with SDPP developed fatal infection. An isolate phylogenetically clustered with South Korea strains. Our findings highlight the need for strengthened risk management of animal-derived feed ingredients like SDPP.

Bacterial competence and genetic diversity: Implications for the design of diagnostics and vaccines.
Bacterial competence and genetic diversity are key determinants of microbial evolution, directly influencing pathogen adaptability, diagnostic reliability, and vaccine effectiveness. Natural transformation, together with horizontal gene transfer and homologous recombination, enables rapid genomic remodeling, facilitating the acquisition of antimicrobial resistance, modification of diagnostic targets, and generation of antigenic variants. These processes are particularly prominent in naturally competent and highly recombining pathogens, where population structures range from clonal to panmictic, shaping responses to selective pressures such as antibiotic use and immunization. This review synthesizes current understanding of the mechanisms governing bacterial competence and their role in generating genomic diversity, with emphasis on implications for diagnostics and vaccine design. Case studies-including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Helicobacter pylori-illustrate how recombination-driven diversification contributes to serotype replacement, diagnostic escape, and variable vaccine performance. Emerging approaches, including pan-genomic target selection, high-throughput sequencing, CRISPR-based diagnostics, and next-generation vaccine platforms, offer strategies to address these challenges but remain constrained by genomic variability and limited global surveillance. We argue that integrating evolutionary dynamics into diagnostic and vaccine development is essential for sustaining effectiveness. Continuous genomic monitoring and adaptive design frameworks will be critical to anticipate and mitigate competence-driven bacterial evolution in clinical and public health settings.

Development and validation of a recombinant chimeric antigen based on Leishmania infantum B-cell epitopes for canine serology.
This study describes the development and validation of a novel multi-epitope chimeric protein (rChi) for the serodiagnosis of canine leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania infantum (CanL). The rChi construct was engineered based on B-cell epitopes from hypothetical proteins previously identified through immunoproteomic profiling. To evaluate its diagnostic performance, an indirect ELISA was conducted using a comprehensive panel of canine serum samples (n = 291), including clinically affected, subclinically infected, and non-infected dogs, as well as Leish-Tec®-vaccinated animals and those infected with potentially cross-reactive pathogens (Babesia vogeli, Ehrlichia canis, and Trypanosoma cruzi). The rChi-ELISA demonstrated superior diagnostic parameters compared to L. infantum soluble Leishmania antigen (SLA), achieving 92.2% sensitivity and 76.2% specificity (AUC = 0.85; Accuracy = 80.8%), whereas SLA showed only 50.0% sensitivity and 68.3% accuracy. These findings indicate that the rChi protein significantly enhances CanL detection and represents a promising tool for more accurate veterinary diagnostics and surveillance.

Well-being and healthcare work over the pandemic.
BACKGROUND: Well-being in the healthcare sector is of substantial policy relevance, given persistent labour shortages and the central role of subjective well-being in worker productivity and retention. OBJECTIVE: We investigate changes in healthcare workers' life satisfaction since the onset of the pandemic relative to workers in other essential and non-essential sectors, and examine the role of pandemic severity and subsequent policy responses in explaining these differences. METHODS: We use thirteen waves of quarterly panel data from the COME-HERE dataset, which collects information on respondents in five European countries from April 2020 to August 2024, and estimate linear regressions via OLS. RESULTS: The life satisfaction of healthcare workers is always higher than that of other essential workers and non-essential workers. During the pandemic, the pandemic death rate had a negative effect on life satisfaction that was three times larger for healthcare workers. At the same time, lockdown stringency reduced the life satisfaction of workers in every sector other than healthcare. CONCLUSIONS: As pandemic death rates and lockdown stringency mostly moved hand-in-hand, the higher life satisfaction of healthcare workers persisted throughout and after the pandemic possibly reflecting the meaningful nature of their jobs. At the same time, the negative impact of pandemic severity on workers' well-being is especially pronounced among healthcare workers, highlighting the importance of supporting their well-being during public health crises to sustain healthcare system performance.

Autoimmune comorbidity profiles in MOGAD and AQP4-NMOSD: a real-world evidence study of top 10 autoimmune disorders across the pre- and post-COVID-19 eras.
INTRODUCTION: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) and aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4-NMOSD) are antibody-mediated demyelinating disorders presenting with distinct immunopathogenic mechanisms. Systemic autoimmune comorbidity patterns and their evolution across the COVID-19 era remain incompletely characterized in real-world settings. We compared systemic autoimmune burdens and immune laboratory profiles between MOGAD and AQP4-NMOSD, systematically evaluating temporal changes before and after the COVID-19 pandemic. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Research Network (2015-2025). Antibody-confirmed cohorts included 2533 MOGAD and 453 AQP4-NMOSD patients (multiple sclerosis was strictly excluded). Ten systemic autoimmune categories were identified using ICD-10 codes. Immune laboratory markers, including antinuclear antibodies, anti-dsDNA, complement levels, and immunoglobulin dynamics, were analyzed. Temporal analyses included pre-/post-diagnosis windows and pre-/post-COVID-19 era stratification. RESULTS: AQP4-NMOSD patients were older and predominantly female compared to those with MOGAD. AQP4-NMOSD demonstrated a substantially higher baseline systemic autoimmune burden, including systemic lupus erythematosus (16%vs 1%), other connective tissue involvement (12%vs 5%), rheumatoid arthritis (6%vs 2%), and autoimmune gastrointestinal disease. Marked serum IgG reduction and post-diagnosis autoantibody titer resolution occurred predominantly in AQP4-NMOSD. COVID-era comparisons revealed persistent, high comorbidity odds in AQP4-NMOSD alongside selective temporal accrual of connective tissue, vascular, and thyroid comorbidities within MOGAD. CONCLUSION: AQP4-NMOSD is embedded within a broader humoral autoimmune network, whereas MOGAD exhibits a restricted systemic immune phenotype. The COVID-19 era accentuated preexisting subtype-specific architectures rather than uniformly increasing autoimmune burden. These findings support subtype-specific autoimmune surveillance strategies and reinforce precision phenotyping in antibody-mediated demyelinating disorders.

Reemergence of DENV-3III_C.1 and emergence of DENV-3III_B.3.2 in Ecuador: multiple introductions and dispersal patterns, 2022-2026.
We characterized the reemergence of DENV-3III_C.1, the emergence of DENV-3III_B.3.2, and their phylogeographic spread in Ecuador during 2022-2026 through integrated epidemiologic and genomic surveillance. Lineage DENV-3III_C.1 formed a monophyletic Ecuadorian cluster closely related to Colombian viruses. The earliest sampled Ecuadorian sequence was detected in Esmeraldas, compatible with a possible introduction across the northern border followed by within-country dissemination. Lineage DENV-3III_B.3.2 comprised multiple Ecuadorian clades related to viruses from Colombia, Cuba, and the United States (travel-associated), consistent with independent introductions followed by geographic expansion. These findings reveal distinct transmission histories and support strengthened genomic surveillance at border crossings and other key points of entry.

Development of a rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay for dual detection of Hantaan virus and Seoul virus.
Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health. Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. Leveraging the programmable precision of CRISPR/Cas12b system, which has significantly advanced the field of molecular diagnostics, we developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV. Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction. The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions. Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1 × 101 copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition. No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. In a preliminary feasibility assessment, all nine RT-qPCR-positive rodent samples (seven HTNV and two SEOV) were positive by the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay, indicating complete positive agreement in this all-positive sample set. Because no negative samples were included, negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed. These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool; larger studies using well-characterized positive and negative clinical or field specimens are required.

Analysis of Lassa Fever Incidence in Nigeria Demonstrates a Clear Climate-Disease Interaction.
Lassa fever remains a major public health concern in Nigeria, where climatic variability, ecological dynamics, and socio-behavioral factors combine to influence transmission patterns. This review synthesizes current evidence on how atmospheric conditions shape Lassa fever incidence through their effects on ecosystems, rodent reservoirs, and human exposure pathways. Drawing on studies in epidemiology, disease ecology, climate science and remote sensing, the review highlights that temperature, rainfall, humidity, vegetation change and large-scale climatic oscillations all contribute to fluctuations in Mastomys natalensis populations which serve as the primary reservoir of Lassa virus. These climatic drivers modify food availability, breeding cycles and habitat suitability for rodents which in turn affect the probability of viral spillover. Modeling approaches including statistical regression, time series analysis, ecological niche modeling and spatiotemporal remote sensing demonstrate that environmental variables significantly improve predictions of disease risk. However, important gaps remain including limited long-term ecological data, underreporting in surveillance systems, insufficient integration of rodent ecology with climate data and a need for more comprehensive socio-behavioral studies. The review recommends future directions such as sustained monitoring of Mastomys populations, high-resolution climate-sensitive modeling, genomic analysis of Lassa virus across climatic gradients and multidisciplinary approaches that combine environmental science with public health research. Improving climate-informed surveillance and early warning systems is essential for strengthening preparedness and reducing the burden of Lassa fever in Nigeria.

RSV, influenza, and COVID-19 in hospitalized children: A comparative analysis of the 2025/2026 epidemic season in Poland.
Comparative data on the epidemiology and clinical impact of RSV, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 infections among hospitalized children during the same epidemic season remain limited in Central Europe. This multicenter retrospective study compared the epidemiological characteristics, clinical presentations, and outcomes of laboratory-confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza, and COVID-19 among hospitalized children in Poland during. A total of 756 patients were evaluated, including 408 with influenza (54.0%), 204 with COVID-19 (27.0%), and 144 with RSV (19.0%). The infections displayed distinct temporal patterns, peaking sequentially from early autumn (COVID-19) through winter (influenza) and early spring (RSV). Demographically, hospitalizations for RSV infection and COVID-19 skewed toward infants and young children (mean ages 1.8 and 2.3 years, respectively), whereas influenza affected a broader age spectrum, extending into (pre)school-aged cohorts (mean age 4.5 years; p < 0.0001). RSV infection was associated with the highest requirement for oxygen support (41.7%) and the longest hospital stay (mean, 6.0 days) compared with influenza and COVID-19 (p < 0.0001). Conversely, pneumonia was most frequently diagnosed in the COVID-19 group (16.2%; p = 0.01), which also exhibited unique elevations in D-dimer levels (p = 0.02). Vaccine and immunoprophylaxis uptake hovered near zero across all cohorts (∼1%). Empirical antibiotic use was highly prevalent (26.6%), exceeding objective pneumonia rates by two-to three-fold. Major pediatric respiratory viruses maintain unique clinical and demographic footprints. The observed low immunization rates and disproportionate antibiotic use underscore an urgent need for targeted pediatric vaccination campaigns and antimicrobial stewardship programs.

The socioeconomic value of adult respiratory vaccination in Australia: a benefit-cost analysis.
BACKGROUND: Pneumococcal disease, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza and COVID-19 cause a major burden of illness and death among adults, much of which is vaccine-preventable. We estimated the societal value of adult vaccination against these four pathogens in Australia. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: We developed disease-specific static life table cohort models and conducted a societal-perspective benefit-cost analysis of adult respiratory vaccination, approximating those recommended by the Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunization, relative to no vaccination. Mortality risk reductions were monetized using value of a statistical life (VSL) and value of a statistical life year (VSLY); avoided morbidity and productivity losses were also captured. Main outcomes were benefit-cost ratios (BCRs) and net monetary benefits (NMBs). RESULTS: Over ten years, age and risk-based vaccination generated gross returns of $11.24 (VSL) and $5.69 (VSLY) per Australian dollar invested (net returns $10.24 and $4.69), with NMBs of $64.97 billion and $29.76 billion, averting 234,187 hospitalizations and 13,890 deaths. BCRs remained well above 1 across all scenarios. CONCLUSIONS: Adult respiratory vaccination shows strong societal returns. Improving coverage and extending eligibility offer the potential for further societal gains. Some simplifications in the model are likely to understate the value of vaccination while others may overstate it.

Genotype-resolved wastewater surveillance for monitoring human norovirus GII circulation.
Norovirus GII causes a substantial global burden of acute gastroenteritis, and genotype-resolved wastewater surveillance offers a complementary approach for monitoring community circulation beyond cases captured by routine clinical surveillance. We monitored four municipal wastewater treatment plants in Beijing, China, from October 2023 to September 2024 and compared weekly GII genotype profiles with contemporaneous sporadic-case and outbreak surveillance. Strict-weekly genotype comparisons were the primary inference and used moving-block bootstrap confidence intervals, block-sign tests, and false-discovery-rate correction; centred 3-week profiles were used for description and sensitivity analysis. Bray-Curtis dissimilarity quantified compositional concordance, and same-week and lagged Spearman correlations compared wastewater GII concentration with clinical surveillance activity. In the centred 3-week wastewater series, GII.4 had the highest mean read-based relative abundance (31.1%), followed by GII.17 (17.5%) and GII.7 (15.2%). In strict-weekly comparisons, wastewater had lower GII.17 representation than sporadic cases (-32.6 percentage points) and lower GII.7 representation than outbreaks (-14.0 percentage points). Wastewater had higher GII.3, GII.4, GII.6, and GII.9 representation than sporadic cases and higher GII.9 and GII.13 representation than outbreaks; the GII.4 and GII.7 differences were sensitive to analytical specification, and the GII.13 effect was small. Mean strict-weekly Bray-Curtis dissimilarities were 0.590-0.679 in 32 common weeks. Same-week and lagged wastewater concentration correlations with sporadic-case positivity and outbreak case counts were not significant after temporal-dependence and multiplicity correction. Genotype-resolved wastewater surveillance documented co-circulating GII genotypes and recurrent source-specific differences, while read-based relative abundance remained dependent on catchment coverage and genotype-specific analytical performance.

Ectromelia Virus Reprograms the Noncanonical NF-κB Signaling Pathway in HeLa Epithelial Cells.
The noncanonical nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) pathway regulates adaptive immune responses and antiviral innate immunity. Orthopoxviruses, including the human pathogen variola virus and zoonotic viruses such as vaccinia virus and monkeypox virus, have evolved multiple strategies to suppress host antiviral signaling. Our previous work using in vitro immune cell models demonstrated that the mouse-specific orthopoxvirus ectromelia virus (ECTV) inhibits the noncanonical NF-κB signaling pathway. Here, we investigated the impact of ECTV on noncanonical NF-κB signaling in human epithelial HeLa cells. Tumor necrosis factor superfamily ligands were used to activate or modulate noncanonical NF-κB signaling. Using fluorescence microscopy and immunoblot analyses, we found that ECTV reduced LIGHT (TNFSF14)- and lymphotoxin α1β2 (LTα1β2)-induced nuclear accumulation of the NF-κB subunits RelB and p52. ECTV infection alone increased whole-cell RelB and NF-κB2/p100 levels but did not significantly alter nuclear RelB levels. In TNF-α-stimulated cells, ECTV reduced levels of cellular inhibitor of apoptosis protein 2 (cIAP2), whereas in LTα1β2-stimulated cells, ECTV reduced levels of TNF receptor-associated factor 3 (TRAF3). RT-qPCR analysis revealed that ECTV upregulated RELB, NFKB2, and CHUK expression. Viral infection also increased expression of TNFAIP3 and OTUD7B, genes encoding regulators of noncanonical NF-κB signaling. Moreover, infected cells exhibited increased expression of selected RelB-responsive genes, including FBRS, CCR10, and TNFRSF6B. Together, these findings indicate that ECTV modulates components associated with noncanonical NF-κB signaling in epithelial cells in vitro, without evidence of constitutive pathway activation.

Of mice and little humans: A comparison of the issues facing drug delivery to wildlife and pediatric patients.
Despite them being two very different patient populations, wildlife and pediatrics share many of the same challenges when it comes to drug development, delivery and the regulatory and clinical factors that impact on development of effective medicines. Drug delivery to wildlife species for prevention and treatment of disease, for conservation or pest control, is an emerging field of research. The current global H5N1 avian flu outbreaks has highlighted zoonotic disease and made us acutely aware of the important link between human health and wildlife health, however effective treatment of wildlife faces significant practical challenges and a paucity of quantitative data. Pediatric patients are also disadvantaged under current development paradigms, in part through ethical hurdles, but also through biopharmaceutical and clinical practice complications. Here, we provide a comparison of the challenges faced with the development of oral formulations for pediatric and wildlife patients and identify areas of translation from one field to the other that can benefit both of these populations. More broadly, realisation of the nexus between prevention of zoonotic diseases and healthy aging from child through to late adulthood is important for the health of humanity in the framework of One Health.

The Risk of an H5N1 Influenza Pandemic.
The last 110 years have seen four influenza A pandemics, where viruses have emerged from mammals or birds with the ability to transmit and cause disease in human populations. Since 2021, a high-pathogenicity strain of avian influenza, H5N1, has caused a panzootic (pandemic of animals), with global spread in wild birds, resulting in frequent spillovers into farmed poultry and into mammals, including mammal species not previously known to be affected by influenza A. This has created increased opportunity for reassortment, mutation, human infection, and potential adaptation to transmit. The risk to humans and the impact are difficult to quantify but of mounting concern to public health bodies. Here, we examine the risk of an H5N1 pandemic emerging and spreading in humans and the potential impact of an H5N1 pandemic.

A caprine mammary infection model for highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus spillover into dairy cows represents the emergence of a mammalian host capable of sustaining a panzootic and creates a transmission pathway to humans. HPAI research involving dairy cows is constrained by the space requirements needed to house large animals in high biocontainment. A small ruminant model would enable larger sample sizes while reducing costs, improving safety, and lowering logistical barriers to conduct research. Here, we establish dairy goats as a model for HPAI mammary infection. Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and genotype B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. Parenteral vaccination with an inactivated virus induced antigen-specific antibodies in blood and milk, reduced clinical disease, limited virus shedding in milk, and mitigated milk production losses. HPAI H5N1 disease dynamics in dairy cows can be recapitulated in dairy goats, providing a relevant model for investigating pathogenesis and for supporting the development of control strategies.

Molecular Detection of Arboviruses in Aedes spp. Larvae During Entomo-Virological Surveillance in a Hospital Area of Brasília, Federal District, Brazil.
BACKGROUND: Arboviruses in hospital environments may represent a neglected risk of nosocomial infections. This study investigated arboviruses in Aedes spp. larvae collected from a hospital area in Brasília, Federal District, Brazil. METHODS: Eighteen ovitraps were deployed for 26 weeks. Hatched Aedes spp. larvae were pooled weekly, and viral detection was performed by reverse transcription-quantitative PCR. RESULTS: Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, and 4, Zika virus, and Chikungunya virus were identified, with an overall positivity rate of 30.76%. CONCLUSION: The surveillance strategy effectively detected arboviral RNA in a hospital setting, suggesting local arboviral circulation associated with the transmission triad.

Resurgence of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo: Lessons Learned and Future Directions.
INTRODUCTION: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains the global epicenter of Ebola virus disease (EVD), having experienced more than 15 outbreaks since the disease was first identified in 1976. The 2025 resurgence in Kasai Province, caused by Orthoebolavirus zairense, resulted in over 60 confirmed cases and a case fatality rate exceeding 65%, highlighting persistent vulnerabilities in outbreak preparedness and response despite previous control successes. This article examines the drivers, response strategies, and public health implications of the 2025 Ebola outbreak. METHODS: This perspective synthesizes evidence from publicly available reports, epidemiological updates, genomic surveillance findings, and guidance from national and international public health agencies to examine the epidemiological characteristics, health system challenges, response interventions, and lessons learned from the 2025 Ebola outbreak in the DRC. RESULTS: Genomic evidence suggested viral persistence in human reservoirs as a likely source of the outbreak. Delayed diagnosis due to limited laboratory capacity, reagent shortages, and slow sample transportation impeded timely case confirmation. Sociocultural factors, including unsafe burial practices, vaccine hesitancy, and community mistrust, further complicated containment efforts. The outbreak overwhelmed fragile health systems, with inadequate isolation facilities and personal protective equipment contributing to healthcare worker infections, which accounted for 10% of reported cases. Coordinated national and international interventions, including emergency response activation, ring vaccination with the rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP (Ervebo) vaccine, enhanced surveillance, contact tracing, infection prevention and control measures, and technical support from global partners, were instrumental in interrupting transmission. CONCLUSION: The 2025 Ebola outbreak demonstrates the continued threat of recurrent EVD in the DRC and underscores the need for resilient surveillance systems, decentralized laboratory capacity, sustained infection prevention and control measures, healthcare worker protection, meaningful community engagement, and strengthened regional collaboration. Integrating genomic surveillance and advancing vaccine research will be critical for improving epidemic preparedness and strengthening health security across Central Africa.

What a highly monitored chikungunya epidemic reveals about preparedness for Europe and beyond.
The 2024-25 chikungunya epidemic in Reunion Island illustrates the challenge of translating early warning into timely public-health action during fast-moving arboviral outbreaks. Despite advanced surveillance, the epidemic accelerated rapidly and placed substantial pressure on primary care. These challenges, together with the complexity of emergency vaccine deployment, highlight the need for anticipatory, integrated preparedness strategies combining surveillance, vaccination, vector control and research.

Early detection of immunoglobulin A against a vaccine backbone protein enables fast, durable, and objective identification of individuals vaccinated against Ebola virus.
BACKGROUND: rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccine is recommended for prevention of Ebola virus (EBOV) infection and disease (EVD). However, breakthrough EBOV infections have been observed in vaccinees. Currently available diagnostic and research assays cannot reliably distinguish individuals vaccinated against Ebola virus from those previously infected with the virus. This limitation complicates interpretation of vaccine-effectiveness studies, seroepidemiologic investigations, and estimates of infection or attack rates. The ability to differentiate vaccine-induced immune responses from those resulting from natural infection remains an important unmet public health and research need. METHODS: We developed a multiplex sero-diagnostic assay simultaneously detecting IgA, IgG, and IgM antibodies against vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus nucleoprotein (VSV-N), a vaccine-specific marker absent in natural infection, and EBOV-GP, the vaccine's target antigen. We evaluated longitudinal samples from 30 individuals after vaccination and 30 placebo (saline) recipients, as well as 8 participants from a long-term vaccination follow-up study. FINDINGS: We detected increase in all antibodies against both protein antigens in vaccinated individuals. Critically, the assay reveals that anti-VSV-N IgA responses emerge earlier and more robustly than anti-GP responses in vaccinees, establishing anti-N IgA as a definitive, early, and durable biomarker of rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccination with high sensitivity and specificity. INTERPRETATION: The assay enables rapid, accurate identification of vaccine recipients and supports real-time assessment of vaccine effectiveness during outbreaks. Furthermore, the assay's adaptability to the expanding pipeline of VSV-vectored vaccines positions it as a transformative diagnostic platform for accelerating preparedness for future infectious disease threats and outbreak response strategies. FUNDING: Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the Divisions of Intramural Research (DIR) and Clinical Research (DCR) of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) at the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Two-Dose Measles-Containing Vaccine (MCV1 and MCV2) Completion and Associated Factors Among Children Aged 24-59 Months in Soroti City, Uganda: A Cross-Sectional Study.
PURPOSE: This study aimed to determine the measles immunization completion rate, defined as receipt of both the first (MCV1) and second (MCV2) doses of measles-containing vaccine, and associated factors among children aged 24-59 months in Soroti City, Northeastern Uganda. PATIENTS AND METHODS: A quantitative analytical cross-sectional study was conducted in Soroti City between November 2025 and January 2026. Multi-stage cluster random sampling was employed to select 325 children aged 24-59 months from households in eight villages across two divisions of Soroti City. Data were collected through face-to-face interviewer-administered questionnaires targeting caregivers. Immunization status was verified using child health cards and, where cards were unavailable, caregiver recall. Data were analyzed using Stata version 15.0, with descriptive statistics, bivariate chi-square tests, and multivariate logistic regression performed at a significance level of p < 0.05. RESULTS: The measles immunization completion rate was 76.6% (95% CI: 71.7-80.9%). Six variables were significantly associated with completion at the bivariate level (p < 0.05) and were entered into the multivariable model: birth order, caregiver occupation, household income, ANC attendance, outreach service availability, and vaccine safety perception. At multivariate analysis, factors independently associated with measles immunization completion were birth order of three and above (AOR = 0.37; 95% CI: 0.15-0.93; p = 0.034), unemployed caregiver occupation (AOR = 2.88; 95% CI: 1.50-5.52; p = 0.002), household income of 200,000-<500,000 UGX (AOR = 0.30; 95% CI: 0.15-0.61; p = 0.001), antenatal care attendance of more than six visits (AOR = 5.77; 95% CI: 1.86-17.93; p = 0.002), availability of outreach services (AOR = 3.82; 95% CI: 1.90-7.70; p < 0.001), and agreement that measles vaccines are safe (AOR = 16.27; 95% CI: 2.83-93.64; p = 0.002). Attendance of 3-6 ANC visits and household income of ≥500,000 UGX were associated with completion at the bivariate level but did not remain statistically significant after adjustment. CONCLUSION: Measles immunization completion among children aged 24-59 months in Soroti City was 76.6%, substantially higher than Uganda's national MR2 uptake of 28% reported for the 2023/2024 financial year, but still below the WHO-recommended 95% threshold; because the national and study estimates refer to different periods and populations, this comparison should be interpreted as indicative rather than a direct benchmark. Outreach service availability, vaccine safety perception, ANC attendance, caregiver occupation, household income, and birth order were the factors most strongly associated with completion in this setting. Strengthening outreach services, integrating immunization counselling into ANC, addressing caregiver concerns about vaccine safety, and paying closer attention to households with several children are programmatic implications suggested by these associations, though intervention effectiveness was not directly tested in this cross-sectional study.

Public Knowledge, Attitudes, and Preventive Practices Regarding Mpox in Bangladesh: Insights From a Community-Based Cross-Sectional Survey.
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Mpox has recently re-emerged as a significant global health concern, highlighting the importance of public awareness and preventive measures. This study aimed to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding Mpox and its epidemiology, prevention, and control measures among the general population of Bangladesh. METHODS: A community-based cross-sectional survey was conducted from June 2024 to September 2024 among 1002 participants across 16 districts, using a multi-stage random sampling approach following STROBE guidelines. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire covering sociodemographics, knowledge, attitudes, and practices. Both univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to determine associations between sociodemographic factors and KAP outcomes. RESULTS: Out of 1002 respondents, only 37.2% demonstrated good knowledge of Mpox, while 74.0% had positive attitudes, and 80.0% reported satisfactory preventive practices. Awareness of Mpox as a viral disease was limited (37.3%), and only 22.5% knew about the protective role of smallpox vaccination. Higher education was strongly associated with good knowledge (AOR = 11.8; 95% CI: 5.61-25.8), positive attitudes (AOR = 5.68; 95% CI: 2.63-12.5), and satisfactory practices (AOR = 6.49; 95% CI: 2.62-16.8). Non-border residents were more likely to report positive attitudes (AOR = 3.07; p < 0.001) and satisfactory practices (AOR = 3.84; p < 0.001). Urban (AOR = 2.28; p = 0.003) and semi-urban (AOR = 2.19; p = 0.014) participants showed more positive attitudes. Attitudes and practices showed the strongest correlation (ρ = 0.793, p < 0.001), indicating a strong association between attitudes and preventive practices. CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that gaps in awareness and training are associated with suboptimal practices, highlighting potential areas for targeted educational interventions. Strengthening community-level awareness and preparedness may support public health readiness for potential Mpox outbreaks in Bangladesh.

Prospective Cardiac MRI study comparing Recovered COVID-19 patients with Recovered Non-COVID-19 Viral Respiratory Infection Patients (R-COVID-CMR).
OBJECTIVE: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has been associated with subclinical myocardial inflammation. Post-COVID-19 infection, there are concerns about subsequent heart failure and persistent myocarditis. It is unknown how COVID-19 infection compares with non-COVID-19 viral infections in terms of myocardial inflammation based on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) assessment. This prospective longitudinal study aims to determine and compare the extent and severity of myocardial involvement in patients with COVID-19 infection versus non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infections (control). METHOD: Recruited recovered COVID-19 (RCOVID) patients and recovered non-COVID (non-COVID) patients from several hospitals and COVID-19-designated clinic underwent three CMR examinations for functional assessment, native T1, T2, and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification, with corroborating blood markers (NT-proBNP, white cell count, c-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and high sensitivity cardiac troponin T). CMR scans took place (i) within 2-week of confirmed recovery, (ii) 3-month, and (iii) 12-month post-recovery. Linear mixed model with Bonferroni correction was used for analysis. RESULTS: 152 participants were recruited, 112 RCOVID outpatients (mean age: 41.0; 58.9% female) and 40 non-COVID inpatients (mean age:45.0; 37.5% female). Non-COVID infections included influenza virus, rhinovirus/enterovirus, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus. At all three time points, blood results and cardiac function parameters were not significantly different between RCOVID and non-COVID patient groups (p-value not significant). Both patient groups had no significant differences for native T1/T2 values, ECV, late gadolinium enhancement, T2 short tau inversion recovery, and overall fulfilment of the 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria at each time points. CONCLUSION: In this prospective longitudinal study with CMR examinations, COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse myocardial inflammatory response than non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infection in terms of CMR parameters, and blood markers. PLAIN ENGLISH SUMMARY: During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreaks, some COVID-19 patients were incidentally found to have inflammation of the muscular layer of the heart. Healthcare professionals were concerned the inflammation will lead to heart not delivering enough blood to meet body demands (ie. heart failure) in the long run. Therefore, we designed this study to better understand the extent and severity of cardiac involvement in patients with COVID-19 by comparing them to patients with other types of viral respiratory infections, such as influenza, which we were more familiar with. We recruited two groups of patients, one group with patients recovered from COVID-19, the other group with patients recovered from other types of viral respiratory infections. For each patient, we arranged three assessments at 2 weeks, 3 months, and 12 months after their recovery respectively. During each assessment, they had blood taken and underwent a cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) scan, a type of medical imaging used for assessment of heart function. 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria (LLC) is a set of criteria for diagnosis of myocardial inflammation recommended by a group of experts. We compared the two groups of patients at each time point according to LLC, as well as their blood markers and heart function. In our study, we found that COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse heart muscle inflammatory response than other types of viral respiratory infections. This is reassuring as patients with previous COVID-19 infections will likely not develop inflammation of the heart muscle nor develop heart failure.

Mpox and sexually transmitted infections: syndemic drivers of transmission and disease outcomes-A Narrative Review.
The worldwide outbreak of mpox (formerly monkeypox) in 2022 emerged as a public health emergency posing greater threat to persons with sexually transmitted infections (STIs). This outbreak featured an increase in overlap between mpox and STIs reflecting evolving transmission dynamics in sexual networks. Epidemiological data reveal that STIs such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Chlamydia trachomatis, herpes simplex virus, syphilis have been frequently associated with mpox infection highlighting the role of sexual contact in its transmission. A narrative review was conducted using PubMed and Google Scholar to identify relevant literature published between 2008 and 2026, focusing on mpox, STIs, co-infections, and pregnancy outcomes. Evidence suggests that biological, behavioural and structural factors may interact to influence mpox transmission and clinical outcomes. STI co-infection may be associated with mucosal invasion and immune modulation plausibly affecting disease progression, however direct mechanistic evidence remains limited. Although mpox infection has majorly affected gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM), its severity in women particularly during pregnancy raises concerns regarding vertical transmission and maternal and neonatal complications. This review highlights current evidence on mpox-STI co-infections, and applies a syndemic framework to interpret their co-occurrence within biological, behavioural and structural contexts. While this perspective provides understanding regarding transmission patterns, further research is needed to establish the extent of these interactions. Recognizing these factors is important for screening, early diagnosis and management strategies to mitigate future outbreaks and impact of mpox. Summary: This narrative review on mpox and STI co-infections explores syndemic interactions, transmission dynamics and implications for disease outcomes and public health management.

Gallbladder Involvement in Pediatric Hepatitis A: Findings From an Italian Outbreak Cohort.
BACKGROUND: Gallbladder involvement during acute hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection is generally considered an uncommon extrahepatic manifestation, although recent reports suggest it may be underrecognized. We evaluated the prevalence, clinical characteristics and outcomes of gallbladder abnormalities in a multicenter cohort of children hospitalized with acute HAV infection during an Italian outbreak. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter observational study, including consecutive children with laboratory-confirmed acute HAV infection admitted to 4 tertiary pediatric hospitals between January and May 2026. Clinical, laboratory and ultrasonographic findings were collected. All patients underwent abdominal ultrasonography during the acute phase of illness. RESULTS: Thirty-three children were included. Gallbladder abnormalities compatible with acute acalculous cholecystitis were identified in 18 patients (54.5%), including marked gallbladder wall thickening (>7 mm) in 8. Children with gallbladder involvement did not exhibit more severe clinical manifestations or greater biochemical impairment than those without ultrasonographic abnormalities. Serum bile acids were markedly elevated in most tested patients but were not associated with gallbladder abnormalities. All patients were managed conservatively, and none developed gallbladder perforation, empyema, gangrene or required surgical intervention. Complete clinical recovery with progressive normalization of laboratory and ultrasonographic findings was observed in all cases. CONCLUSIONS: Systematic ultrasonography identified gallbladder involvement in more than half of children hospitalized with acute HAV infection, suggesting that this manifestation may be substantially underrecognized rather than truly rare. Despite frequent ultrasonographic abnormalities, the clinical course was uniformly benign, supporting conservative management in the absence of complications.

Disclosing pathogenic processes of monkeypox (MPOX) and drug repurposing through host-transcriptomics analysis.
Monkeypox (MPOX) virus infection outbreak in Africa in 2022 was initially considered a neglected tropical disease (NTD). Now it is recognized as a global health problem. The recent global spread has emphasized the need for increased attention to combat MPOX. Although there are some vaccines against MPOX, most people worldwide are still not vaccinated due to their unawareness or unavailability. However, so far, there is no approved drug against MPOX yet. Therefore, effective drugs against MPOX are also essential. This study attempted to disclose pathogenic processes and therapeutic strategies of MPOX based on MPOX-associated host key-genes (hKGs). At first, three transcriptomic profile datasets were analyzed, identifying 166 common host differentially expressed genes (hDEGs) between MPOX patients and control groups, comprising 75 upregulated and 91 downregulated hDEGs. Subsequently, six top-ranked host key genes (hKGs): ALB, HSP90AA1, CDH1, PTPRC, IGF1, and ABL1, were identified as potential MPOX-causing genes through protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis. Functional enrichment analysis of these hKGs revealed critical pathogenic processes of MPOX infection, including biological processes, molecular functions, cellular components, and KEGG pathways. Regulatory network analysis involving transcription factors and miRNAs provided further insights into disease mechanisms. Based on molecular docking analysis, five top-ranked drug molecules Tecovirimat, Beclabuvir, Maraviroc, Raltegravir, and Brincidofovir were identified as potential repurposable therapeutics against MPOX. ADME/T and drug-likeness evaluations confirmed favorable pharmacokinetic properties for these candidates. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the top three complexes (ALB-Tecovirimat, CDH1-Maraviroc, and PPARG-Beclabuvir) demonstrated strong binding stability, supported by RMSD, RMSF, and MM-GBSA results. Therefore, the results provided in this study might be potential resources for diagnosis and therapies of MPOX patients. However, the findings require experimental validation in wet lab for further confirmation.

Owned dog population profile, dog ownership and bite risk determinants: Key steps to rabies control in Antananarivo, Madagascar.
Rabies remains a significant public health threat in Madagascar, with dog-mediated transmission causing approximately 1,000 human deaths annually. In Antananarivo, the capital city, control efforts are hindered by limited up to date knowledge on the dog population. This study aims to provide updated estimates of the owned dog population characteristics, identify determinants of ownership, and assess dog bite incidence and risk factors to guide effective vaccination and prevention strategies. Between 2023 and 2025, a longitudinal door‑to‑door household survey was conducted across 21 fokontany (administrative units) in Antananarivo. Of 2,518 surveyed households, 30.5% reported dog ownership, with 1,273 dogs recorded, yielding an estimated dog‑to‑human ratio of 1:9. The owned dog population was predominantly male (63.6%), with a median age of three years. Survival analysis in the selected study site indicated a median lifespan of 4.4 years and an annual mortality hazard of 16%. Vaccination coverage was low: 64.2% of owned dogs had never been vaccinated, primarily due to owners' time constraints, lack of awareness about the need for dog rabies vaccination, and financial barriers. Ownership was positively associated with household location and size, household head's age, education and income. No significant difference in bite risk was observed between dog‑owning and non‑dog‑owning households, whereas households with children under 15 years experienced a significantly higher risk. Rabies elimination among the owned dog population in Antananarivo requires sustained, context‑adapted interventions that address high population turnover. Annual city‑wide dog vaccination campaigns combining door‑to‑door strategies with fixed‑point sites are suggested to increase the chances of reaching a larger share of the owned dog population. Public health efforts must also prioritize paediatric bite prevention and expand access to post‑exposure prophylaxis to contribute to the global goal of eliminating dog‑mediated human rabies by 2030.

Molecular screening of selected RNA viruses in neotropical wild felids of Brazil.
Astrovirus, cardiovirus and rotavirus are RNA viruses widely distributed among humans, domestic and wild mammals, including felids, occasionally associated with fatal outbreaks and highly resistant to environmental conditions. Despite this, there are no reports of these viruses in New World felids. The aim of this study was to investigate the presence of astrovirus, rotavirus and cardiovirus in non-domestic felids under human care or in the wild, across multiple Brazilian biomes (i.e., Amazon Forest, Atlantic Forest, Caatinga, and Cerrado). Biological samples (e.g., blood, oral and rectal swabs, and frozen tissues) were submitted to reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for astrovirus detection and real-time RT-PCR for rotavirus and cardiovirus, followed by sequencing. Fifty wild felids were analyzed, comprising 40 free-ranging and 10 captive animals: 19 ocelots (Leopardus pardalis), 12 pumas (Puma concolor), seven jaguarundis (Herpailurus yagouaroundi), six southern tiger cats (Leopardus guttulus), three margays (Leopardus wiedii) and three jaguars (Panthera onca). An astrovirus was detected in rectal swab of a healthy captive southern tiger cat, while a genotype G3P[3] Rotavirus alphagastroenteritidis (Rotavirus A) was detected in intestine of a roadkill puma. All felid samples were negative for cardiovirus. Morphological analyses of available formalin-fixed tissues of the rotavirus-positive puma were inconclusive due to autolysis. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first molecular detection of astrovirus and rotavirus in Neotropical wild felid species.

Epidemiological and sociodemographic profile of Mpox in Brazilian Amazon: a cross-sectional study.
BACKGROUND: The Mpox outbreak was characterized by viral transmission within sexual networks and atypical clinical presentations, requiring regional epidemiological evaluations. This study aimed to describe the sociodemographic profile, temporal notification trends, and clinical characteristics of suspected and confirmed Mpox cases in Pará, Brazilian Amazon (2022-2025). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Observational, cross-sectional, and analytical study based on the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN) between March 2022 and December 2025, adhering to STROBE guidelines. The sample (N = 296) was stratified into confirmed Mpox cases (G1; n = 86) and ruled-out cases (G2; n = 210). Associations were evaluated using Pearson's Chi-square test (for expected cell counts ≥ 5) or Fisher's exact test (for expected counts < 5), with significance set at p < 0.05 in SPSS v.26.0. RESULTS: In G1, infection was concentrated among men (97.7%), cisgender men (96.5%), adults aged 19 to 59 years (98.8%), residents of Belém (76.7%), individuals with tertiary education (53.5%), and those reporting homosexual (73.3%) or bisexual (12.8%) orientation (p < 0.001). Clinically, fever (81.4%; p < 0.001) and localized genital lesions (43.0% in G1 vs. 6.2% in G2; p < 0.001) were the primary presentations. Intimate sexual contact was the primary probable exposure pathway (65.1%; p < 0.001). A high proportion of HIV coinfection was observed in G1 (54.7%), with complete reporting overlap with immunosuppression status, alongside 23.3% presenting an active STI at notification (p < 0.001), predominantly active syphilis (16.3%). Clinical management was predominantly outpatient (7.0% hospitalization rate; p = 0.261), with a 96.5% cure rate among valid confirmed cases. No Mpox-attributed deaths occurred among confirmed cases, though all-cause mortality in G1 was 2.3% (n = 2). CONCLUSION: Mpox cases in Pará were concentrated in the state capital, associated with intimate sexual contact networks among young adults, and characterized by high coinfection frequencies with HIV and syphilis.

Oncolytic virotherapy for cancer: biological mechanisms, clinical advances, and future perspectives.
Oncolytic virotherapy has emerged as a promising cancer treatment that combines selective tumor destruction with potent stimulation of antitumor immunity. Unlike conventional therapies, oncolytic viruses (OVs) preferentially infect and replicate within malignant cells while sparing normal tissues, leading to direct tumor lysis and the release of tumor-associated antigens, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, and damage-associated molecular patterns that activate both innate and adaptive immune responses. Advances in molecular virology and genetic engineering have transformed naturally occurring viruses into programmable therapeutic platforms capable of delivering immunomodulatory payloads that enhance antitumor efficacy and remodel the tumor microenvironment. Multiple DNA- and RNA-based viral platforms, including herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, vaccinia virus, reovirus, measles virus, Newcastle disease virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, and coxsackievirus, are currently under clinical investigation, with regulatory approval of talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) and G47Δ providing important proof of clinical feasibility. Increasing evidence indicates that OVs can convert immunologically "cold" tumors into "hot" tumors, thereby improving responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors and other therapeutic modalities. Consequently, oncolytic virotherapy has become an attractive component of combination strategies involving immunotherapy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapies, and cellular therapies. Nevertheless, several challenges continue to limit its broader clinical application, including antiviral immune clearance, inefficient systemic delivery, restricted intratumoral spread, tumor heterogeneity, manufacturing complexity, and the lack of robust predictive biomarkers. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the biological foundations of oncolytic virotherapy, viral engineering strategies, mechanisms of tumor selectivity, direct oncolysis, immunogenic cell death, and immune remodeling of the tumor microenvironment.
