This is linked to the NDV significant genetic variability, its capacity to evolve under selective pressure and its wide range of natural hosts, with diverse virus variants continuing to circulate globally in both domestic and wild birds. Wild synanthropic and migratory birds play an important role in maintaining the virus and transmitting it across regions and continents. Summarized monitoring data from different countries evidences global picture of up-to-date virus distribution and changes in the different virus variant composition from 2017-2026. Some commonly used tests may miss newly emerging variants, and diagnostic procedures thus have to be regularly modified.

Biosecurity risk factors associated with outbreaks of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) on poultry farms in Lower Saxony (Germany) - A case-control-study.
Biosecurity is an essential component when considering risk factors for high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) and may be an explanation for the phenomenon that not all poultry farms are equally affected by outbreaks - despite similar conditions in terms of location, surroundings and size as well as type of poultry and production. In a case-control study, the association of biosecurity measures with the risk of outbreaks of HPAI in poultry farms in Lower Saxony, Germany, was investigated. In total 15 case farms with at least two previous outbreaks of HPAI and 26 control farms without such were examined during farm visits using a specially developed biosecurity checklist. In the univariable logistic regression analysis, the following factors showed a significant association with the outbreak status in poultry farms: longer distance to nearest federal highways, not short-cut grass areas around the stables, no dedicated facilities for removing carcasses from the stables, using trays instead of mats for shoe disinfection as well as feed, litter and manure storage in such a way that suppliers have to enter the clean area. In the multivariable analysis with backward stepwise regression only the variables not short-cut grass areas and no dedicated facilities for removing carcasses from the stables were identified as factors having a significant association with the HPAI outbreak status of a poultry farm. Taking these factors into account could contribute to reducing the risk of HPAI on poultry farms.

THRESHER: A tool for evidence-based, phylogeny-corrected SNP thresholds for whole genome molecular epidemiology.
Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is the gold standard for bacterial pathogen surveillance, where transmission is commonly inferred by calculating pairwise single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and applying a fixed threshold below which two genomes are considered the "same" strain. Such cutoffs are largely arbitrary. The relationship between genetic distance and epidemiological linkage varies with sample size, sampling duration, setting, and patterns of infection and carriage. A threshold calibrated in one study may not transfer to another. To address this, we present THRESHER, a pipeline that infers data-driven phylothresholds directly from each dataset's genomic structure. THRESHER implements four endpoint methods, plateau, public, peak , and discrepancy , with each reflecting a distinct hypothesis about what constitutes the "sameness" of a strain. Across 55 published datasets spanning Staphylococcus aureus, Clostridioides difficile , and Klebsiella pneumoniae , THRESHER reproduced the originally reported strain compositions in smaller studies. In larger studies, where the two diverged, SNP distances and phylogenetic topology supported THRESHER's assignments. In simulated populations with known strain structure, THRESHER recovered transmission clusters with substantially higher sensitivity than fixed cutoffs while retaining high specificity.

Longitudinal personal environmental exposure and Streptococcus pneumoniae colonisation in a cohort of children 5-14 years old in rural Gambia.
BACKGROUND: Air pollution contributes substantially to morbidity and mortality in low-income countries, where reliance on solid fuels leads to high levels of household exposure. Colonisation of the upper respiratory tract by Streptococcus pneumoniae is a prerequisite for pneumococcal disease, and inhaled air pollutants may influence colonisation through impaired mucociliary clearance. Therefore, we investigated the association between S. pneumoniae colonisation and personal exposure to particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) and carbon monoxide (CO) as well as temperature and relative humidity in older children in The Gambia. METHODS: We conducted a prospective study of 134 children aged 5-14 years across eight visits in rural Gambia. Personal 24-hour PM 2.5 , CO, temperature and relative humidity exposures were measured using personal monitors. Concurrently, combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swabs were collected at each visit, and S. pneumoniae colonisation was determined by microbiological culture. Mixed-effects logistic regression models were used to examine associations between environmental exposures and colonisation. Exposures were additionally decomposed into between-child and within-child components. Models were adjusted for age, season, and household income tertile. RESULTS: A total of 554 child visits with paired exposure and microbiological data were analysed. Overall, 24-hour geometric mean PM 2.5 and CO were 12.6 µg/m³ (95% CI 12.2-13.1) and 0.16 ppm (95% CI 0.14-0.19) respectively and overall S. pneumoniae colonisation prevalence was 39.7%. In conventional models, PM 2.5 , CO, temperature, and relative humidity were not significantly associated with S. pneumoniae colonisation after adjustment for confounders. In the within-between decomposition analysis, higher between-child temperature exposure was consistently associated with lower odds of colonisation (mutually adjusted model: OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.56-0.98; p = 0.034). Relative humidity showed an inverse within-child association in crude analysis (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52-0.93; p = 0.013), which attenuated after adjustment for season and other confounders. No associations were observed for PM 2.5 or CO exposures. CONCLUSION: At the exposure levels observed in this cohort of older children, PM 2.5 and CO exposures were not independently associated with S. pneumoniae colonisation. The pattern observed for temperature suggests that longer-term temperature conditions may be more relevant to pneumococcal colonisation than short-term exposure variation in this setting.

The relationship between cross-reactive Plasmodium vivax antibody responses and P. knowlesi parasitaemia and clearance.
Background Pre-existing antibodies to Plasmodium vivax may cross-react with P. knowlesi and influence infection outcomes. We investigated whether baseline P. vivax antibody levels affect parasitaemia and clearance in knowlesi malaria. Methods Total IgG to 21 P. vivax antigens was quantified in pre-treatment plasma from patients in three Malaysian clinical trials. Parasitaemia was assessed 6-hourly by microscopy and clearance half-life estimated. Antibody associations with P. knowlesi baseline parasitaemia and clearance were identified using regression and machine learning approaches (elastic net regression and random forests). Results Data were available for 134 patients (median age 37 years, 37% with prior malaria). Five antibodies were associated with reduced baseline P. knowlesi parasitaemia (0.75-0.90-fold lower per two-fold increase, 95% CIs ranging from 0.65-1.00). Median P. knowlesi parasite clearance half-life was 2.6 hours (IQR 2.1-3.2). Two antibodies were associated with slightly slower parasite clearance (1.04-fold increases in mean clearance half-life per two-fold antibody level). Within-group correlation analyses revealed widespread, positive antibody associations in P. knowlesi infections, with weaker but coordinated (RBP and DBP family) responses in malaria-negative endemic controls. Conclusions Cross-reactive P. vivax antibodies may partially constrain P. knowlesi parasitaemia, but functional studies are needed to clarify their role in immunity and zoonotic transmission.

BTV-3 vaccination decisions among German livestock farmers: a KAP survey.
Following the emergence of Bluetongue virus serotype 3 (BTV-3) in Germany in late 2023, thousands of outbreaks were reported nationwide during 2024, posing a substantial threat to livestock farming. In response, preventive vaccination was recommended and implemented on a voluntary basis. This study examined German livestock farmers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) related to BTV-3 vaccination. An online questionnaire was distributed nationwide in November and December 2024 to assess farmers' willingness to vaccinate and to identify factors influencing vaccination decisions. A total of 1965 livestock holders participated. More than half reported fully vaccinating all their animals against BTV-3 in 2024. Vaccination uptake was significantly higher in conventional compared to organic farms and among small ruminant farms compared to cattle farms. In a logistic regression model, higher knowledge levels regarding BTV and vaccination were positively associated with vaccination uptake. Geographic variation was also observed, with lower vaccination uptake in southern regions of Germany. Participants most frequently reported preventing mortality and clinical disease, as well as avoiding economic losses, as reasons for vaccinating their animals. Around one third of participants did not vaccinate their animals in 2024, with most commonly reported barriers being concerns about vaccine side effects and economic considerations. Perceived lack of information about safety and effectiveness of vaccines may have contributed additionally to hesitancy among farmers. Financial incentives, recommendations from veterinarians, and the possibility of combined vaccination against several serotypes were identified as key factors that could encourage future vaccination. These findings indicate that knowledge gaps and economic constraints hindered widespread BTV-3 vaccination among livestock farmers in Germany in 2024. Targeted information campaigns, financial incentives, and strengthened veterinary guidance are essential to improve vaccination acceptance and enhance future bluetongue control efforts.

Rising spillover risk: Lessons from the Andes hantavirus outbreak.
The unprecedented expansion of human activity boundaries is turning spillover from a chance event into a foreseeable ecological and epidemiological certainty. Using the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak as an entry point, this study examines it within a broader driver framework: nearly all emerging infectious disease events in humans in recent decades have originated from wildlife transmission; under climate-change and land-use scenarios, approximately 3139 mammal species are projected to aggregate in new combinations by 2070, causing an estimated 4000 cross-species viral transmission events. The rapid expansion of tourism into ecologically fragile regions - sub-Antarctic waters, the deep sea, and primary forests - the persistence of habitat fragmentation and animal trade, and the reshaping of wildlife distribution and vector dynamics by extreme climate events together constitute "novel contact amplifiers" that accelerate contact at the human-animal-environment interface. Robotics, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving, and automated logistics are extending human activities into previously inaccessible regions, yet they remain almost entirely absent from current spillover risk assessments. The limitations of cruise ship medical systems - whose core capacity lies in "recognize, isolate, stabilize, and transfer" rather than definitive diagnosis and treatment - were fully exposed in this event. From a One Health perspective, this paper proposes that responses to spillover risk must shift from passive reaction to proactive interface governance, incorporate technology-driven increases in contact frequency into prevention and control frameworks, and advance cornerstone strategies such as broad-spectrum vaccines and broad-spectrum antiviral drugs at the basic research level.

Dengue virus 1 and 2: Epidemiology, host-virus interactions, clinical severity and integrated control strategies.
Dengue is a serious mosquito-borne viral disease caused by four antigenically distinct serotypes of the dengue virus, of which DENV-1 and DENV-2 have been found to play significant roles in outbreaks and severe disease across different geographical areas. This review discusses the epidemiology, host-virus interactions, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, severity, vaccination, and integrated control strategies of DENV-1 and DENV-2. The relevant literature was identified by searching major scientific databases using keywords related to DENV-1, DENV-2, dengue epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical severity, immune responses, vaccination, and vector control; studies were selected for relevance to the review's objectives. The evidence suggests that DENV-1 and DENV-2 share a number of major mechanisms in causing disease, including viral replication, innate immune modulation, endothelial dysfunction mediated by viral NS1, inflammatory response, and antibody-dependent enhancement, but that clinical outcomes are variable and may depend on viral genotype/lineage, prior dengue exposure, host immunity, age, geographical context, and study population. Furthermore, epidemiological and clinical studies have been unable to rank the severity of DENV-1 and DENV-2, as both serotypes have been reported to cause severe dengue across different settings and conditions. The available data thus suggest that the severity of dengue is multifactorial and not serotype-dependent. Ongoing comparative studies that integrate viral genetics, host immune responses, epidemiology, vaccines, and vector control are needed to enhance serotype-specific dengue prevention and clinical management.

[Epidemiological characteristics and response measures of Chikungunya fever in Foshan City, Guangdong Province, 2025].
Objective: To analyze the epidemiological characteristics and response measures of Chikungunya fever in Foshan City in 2025, providing reference for optimizing the prevention and control strategies of vector-borne diseases in China. Methods: Data on locally acquired Chikungunya fever cases reported in Foshan City from July to October 2025 were collected. Descriptive epidemiology and spatial autocorrelation analysis were used to analyze case characteristics at each stage. Results: A total of 10 804 locally acquired Chikungunya fever cases were reported in Foshan City from July to October 2025. The interval from the onset of the earliest traceable case to the identification of the index case was 22 days. The epidemic was divided into the initial response stage (July 8 to July 16), the intensive control stage (July 17 to August 19), and the consolidation stage (August 20 to October 31). A statistically significant difference in the age distribution of cases was observed across the three stages (χ2=49.26, P 0 (range: 0.17-0.65, P<0.05) for all three stages. High-high clustering areas shifted from 3 towns/subdistricts in Shunde District northward to 4 towns/subdistricts in Nanhai District, 3 towns/subdistricts in Chancheng District, and 1 town/subdistrict in Shunde District. Key control measures during the intensive control stage included activating a municipal level Ⅲ public health emergency response, launching citywide campaigns to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, implementing intensive adult mosquito eradication actions, and conducting a nail-removal operation in key villages/communities. During the consolidation stage, the qualified rates for the breteau index and the adult mosquito density index in affected villages/communities reached 99.18% and 98.79%, respectively; the interval from onset to reporting was shortened to 1.38 (0.97, 2.19) days, and the proportion of villages/communities that had ended the outbreak reached 55.88%. Conclusions: The Chikungunya fever epidemic in Foshan City from July to October 2025 was large in scale, widespread, and spatially clustered. Epidemiological characteristics varied across different stages. Implementing staged and differentiated control strategies was important to effectively containing the outbreak within a relatively short period.

Long-term Rotarix Vaccine Effectiveness in Coastal Kenya, Estimated From Child Hospital Admissions Data From July 2014 to December 2022.
BACKGROUND: Two doses of Rotarix demonstrated approximately 64% effectiveness against rotavirus hospitalization in Kenyan children 2.5 years postintroduction. We evaluated long-term Rotarix effectiveness and monitored circulating genotypes over its 8.5 years of use in Kenya. METHODS: We conducted a test-negative case-control study in coastal Kenya among children admitted to Kilifi County Referral Hospital with diarrhea from July 2014 to December 2022. Eligible children had known Rotarix vaccination status, parent/guardian consent, and rotavirus testing via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Positives were genotyped by sequencing. Rotarix effectiveness was estimated using unconditional logistic regression, adjusting for age, sex, calendar year, seasonality, and nutritional status. RESULTS: Of the 1104 children (median age, 12 months [interquartile range, 8-18 months]) included in the effectiveness analysis, 87% (962/1104) had received 2 doses, 6% (70/1104) 1 dose, and 7% (72/1104) zero doses. Rotavirus was detected in stool specimens of 147 (13%) children. Overall, adjusted 2-dose Rotarix effectiveness was 68% (95% confidence interval [CI], 42%-82%). Effectiveness in children aged <12 months was 83% (95% CI, 62%-93%) compared to 38% (95% CI, -106% to 78%) in children aged ≥12 months. Genotyping of 147 positive samples revealed G3P[8] (66/147 [44.9%]), G1P[8] (32/147 [21.8%]), and G2P[4] (23/147 [15.6%]) to be the most common circulating rotavirus genotypes during the Rotarix vaccination era. CONCLUSIONS: Rotarix maintained modest effectiveness in coastal Kenya during its 8.5 years of use. Effectiveness declined in the second year of life onward, probably reflecting a combination of both waning immunity and accumulation of natural immunity among unvaccinated children. Emergence of vaccine heterologous strains emphasizes the need for continued effectiveness surveillance.

Emerging zoonotic diseases management: designing One Health interventions through a community lens including mental health.
INTRODUCTION: The One Health (OH) approach has emerged as a comprehensive approach that recognizes the complexity of health challenges. Previous global health emergencies including Ebola and Covid-19 caused major social and psychological disruptions, generating fear, stigma, distrust, denial of disease and resistance to control measures. This study aims to investigate stakeholder OH perspectives and to assist in designing adaptations for interventions through a community lens, including for mental health. METHODS: This mixed-methods study draws upon OH coordination activities and field experiences in Senegal and has been conducted between 2022 and 2024. Data sources include records of activities implemented through the National OH platform, epidemiological investigations carried out in collaboration with the Institut Pasteur de Dakar and the Ministry of Health and Social Action, and subsequent field investigations conducted in 2024. Qualitative information has been collected through participatory observation, field reports from eight OH coordination meetings, and nine semi-structured interviews conducted during the epidemiological investigations. In addition, 35 key informant interviews have been conducted with governmental, institutional, and community stakeholders involved in epidemic preparedness and response. Narrative accounts have been collected from 27 patients, survivors, and caregivers in relation to Covid-19, rabies, and Crimean Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF), as well as from four livestock keepers who had experienced animal losses. Quantitative data have been obtained through a survey of 434 livestock keepers assessing their knowledge, perceptions, and practices related to zoonotic diseases and OH interventions. RESULTS: The study has identified several indicators of psychosocial distress among affected individuals and communities. Analysis of the OH coordination platform has shown that emergency responses were primarily organized around collaboration between the human, animal, and environmental health sectors, with operational activities mainly focused on surveillance, case detection, and contact tracing. Yet, social scientists, psychologists, and social workers were rarely involved in preparedness and outbreak responses. The study also revealed limited knowledge of zoonotic diseases among livestock keepers, with the majority (89.86%) recognizing only one or two diseases. Low knowledge was significantly associated with lower levels of formal education (p < 0.03). However, respondents demonstrated local knowledge of these diseases, describing some of them using local names. Most respondents (87.1%) reported no prior knowledge of the OH approach, while 75.81% were aware that diseases could be transmitted from animals to humans. CONCLUSION: The study suggests that OH interventions should be designed to bridge central decision making, operational planning, and community realities by integrating local knowledge, strengthening cross-sectoral collaboration and incorporating psychosocial dimensions into epidemic preparedness and response strategies.

Psychotropic prescribing trends in a Peruvian General Hospital during and after the COVID-19 pandemic: an interrupted time-series analysis.
PURPOSE: To evaluate trends in psychotropic prescription rates (PRs) in a Peruvian general hospital during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted an interrupted time-series (ITS) study using routinely collected clinical data from hospitalized patients with psychiatric diagnoses between September 2020 and December 2024. Psychotropic PRs, defined as the number of weekly psychotropic prescriptions per 1,000 psychiatric consultations, were calculated overall and by subclass: antidepressants (N06A), antipsychotics (N05A), anxiolytics (N05B), and mood stabilizers (N05AN01/N03A). For ITS analysis, the study period was divided into six predefined phases (two waves, three relaxation phases, and one post-pandemic phase) based on COVID-19 mortality and transmission trends in Peru. Segmented regression models were applied to estimate phase-specific level and slope changes. RESULTS: A total of 6,151 patients were included. The overall psychotropic PR was higher during the post-pandemic period compared with the pandemic period (1,308 vs. 1,254; p = 0.023). ITS analyses showed a significant downward trend in overall psychotropic prescribing during phase 1 (post-first wave stabilization, β = -25.53; 95% CI = -43.82 to -7.01; p = 0.007), followed by a structural break in phase 2 (second pandemic wave) with an abrupt level increase (β = 295.53; 95% CI = 60.48 to 530.57; p = 0.014) and slope reversal (β = 23.79; 95% CI = 3.33 to 44.26; p = 0.016), after which prescribing stabilized. A similar temporal pattern was observed for antidepressant PR. Anxiolytic PR displayed a transient upward slope change in phase 2 (β = 14.15; 95% CI = 1.80 to 26.50; p = 0.01), whereas antipsychotic and mood stabilizer prescribing remained stable across phases. CONCLUSIONS: Overall psychotropic prescribing showed phase-specific disruption followed by structural rebound and subsequent stabilization across the COVID-19 and post-pandemic periods. These findings provide real-world evidence and underscore the need to monitor psychiatric prescribing and mental health service adaptation in middle-income settings.

Case Report: Sustained pubertal suppression for 68 months with a single histrelin acetate implant in central precocious puberty.
The subcutaneous histrelin acetate implant is FDA-approved for 12 months of continuous gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist therapy in central precocious puberty (CPP). Published data demonstrated sustained suppression with a single implant for up to approximately 24 months; however, efficacy beyond this duration has not been reported. A 7 years 5 month old female patient presented with bilateral Tanner 2 breast development, a bone age of 10 years, and laboratory findings consistent with early central activation. Treatment was delayed 11 months due to disruptions in care during the COVID-19 pandemic, and a histrelin implant was placed at age 8 years 5 months. The patient was lost to follow-up and returned at nearly 14 years of age, approximately 68 months after the implant placement, with primary amenorrhea and pubertal arrest. Laboratory evaluation before implant removal showed suppressed but detectable gonadotropins with a prepubertal estradiol, consistent with sustained partial suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis sufficient to arrest pubertal progression. Her predicted adult height (PAH) of 167.6 cm (66 inches) approximated her mid-parental height (MPH) of 166.4 cm (65.5 inches). This case demonstrates that a single histrelin acetate implant may maintain clinically meaningful pubertal suppression for at least 68 months. These findings support broader investigations into the pharmacokinetics of extended implant use, given implications for reducing surgical burden and healthcare costs in CPP management.

Immunomodulatory RIG-I Agonist SLR14 Confers Protection Against a Range of Highly Pathogenic Negative Sense RNA viruses.
Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs. Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses. SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically. In vivo , a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice. Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation. Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.

A High-Content Pseudotime Framework for Morphological Profiling of Dengue Virus Inhibitors from a Drug-Repurposing Library.
UNLABELLED: Dengue virus (DENV) causes dengue fever, a globally prevalent, epidemic-prone disease with no FDA-approved antivirals. Additionally, the available vaccine for DENV can increase the risk of severe dengue fever for those who have never had a DENV infection due to antibody-dependent enhancement. Thus, there is an urgent need to identify DENV antivirals. Drug repurposing, high-content screening, and machine learning were leveraged to efficiently identify antivirals likely to inhibit DENV replication. Using high-content screening in a DENV infection model, we characterized the morphological patterns of NS4B and envelope (E) protein expression over time and developed a viral pseudotime model that predicts infection progression to aid in phenotypic interpretation of drug effects. We then developed a single cell infection classifier for antiviral efficacy and performed high-throughput drug screening of 960 compounds. We identified four concentration-dependent inhibitors of DENV with nanomolar-to-submicromolar potencies: esomeprazole, GW4064, pralatrexate, and LY411575. With our pseudotime machine learning model trained on data from the time-series assay, we scored the concentration-dependent inhibitors to map their mode of action onto time points in the viral life cycle. Our most notable results show that LY411575, a gamma secretase inhibitor, exhibited an IC 50 of 72 nM and reduced percent infection to near the level of the mock infection control. Pseudotime inferences generated mode of action predictions that were supported by time-of-addition experiments, indicating that LY411575 arrests DENV infection before the development of late-stage infection associated morphologies, while retaining activity when added after inoculation. IMPORTANCE: Our approach reported herein couples high-content screening and a viral pseudotime model as a robust platform for the identification of viral inhibitors with imputation of morphological profiles for large-scale drug discovery efforts. Viral pseudotime models can, in principle, be developed for any viruses or biological processes through a defined life cycle, suggesting that phenotypic time points, or phases, can be mapped across data in a broad range of applications. We report a high-content pseudotime framework for mapping temporal phenotypes and apply it to drug repurposing for DENV antivirals, gaining insight into how the mode of action of the screened antivirals correlates to phases of DENV replication. This study demonstrates how image-derived phenotypes can be leveraged to generate mode of action hypotheses and prioritize antiviral candidates for follow-up studies.

Phenuivirus glycoprotein Gc domain is a conserved target of cross-functional monoclonal antibodies.
Phenuiviruses which include Rift Valley Fever Virus (RVFV), classified by WHO as one of the top priority pathogens with outbreak potential, are emerging arthropod-borne viruses that pose an increasing threat to public health. In line with the "prototype pathogen" framework advanced by the NIAID, the sandfly-transmitted Toscana virus (TOSV) has been adopted as a prototype to advance understanding of relevant phenuiviruses and inform the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. In this study, we sought to isolate and characterize monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) elicited by natural TOSV infection to identify shared antigenic determinants. By employing the conserved envelope Gc glycoprotein as bait for antigen-specific B cell sorting, we recovered more than 1,450 memory B cells and identified 112 Gc-specific neutralizing mAbs. Over one-third of these mAbs exhibited cross-reactivity with RVFV, a genetically distinct phenuivirus. Selected mAbs provided prophylactic protection in a murine model of TOSV infection. Together, our findings establish Gc as an important target of protective neutralizing antibodies and provide insights that may guide the rational design of widely effective interventions, strengthening readiness against future phenuivirus outbreaks.

Integrated proteomic and metabolomic profiling characterizes tryptophan metabolic disturbance associated with mortality in ICU-admitted SFTS patients.
Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Dabie bandavirus, is associated with high mortality among intensive care unit (ICU) patients; however, the integrated proteomic-metabolomic mechanisms underlying fatal outcomes remain poorly characterized. This prospective cohort study enrolled 68 patients with SFTS, who were admitted to the ICU and classified them as survivors (n = 33) or non-survivors (n = 35) according to their 28-day clinical outcomes. Untargeted metabolomic profiling using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry and quantitative proteomic profiling using data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry were performed on plasma samples collected at ICU admission. Multivariable analysis, pathway enrichment analysis, correlation analysis, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis were used to identify potential prognostic biomarkers and characterize molecular associations. Non-survivors exhibited more severe multi-organ injury and systemic inflammation. Metabolomic profiling revealed marked disruption of tryptophan metabolism: L-tryptophan levels were decreased, whereas kynurenine and its downstream metabolites (kynurenic acid [KA], 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid [3-HAA], xanthurenic acid [XA], and 5-hydroxyindolepyruvate [5-HIP]) were increased, suggesting activation of the kynurenine pathway. The four core tryptophan metabolites yielded a combined area under the curve (AUC) of 0.934 for predicting 28-day mortality and were correlated with indicators of renal function and coagulation. Proteomic profiling identified 200 differentially expressed proteins: proteins upregulated in survivors were enriched in the proteasome pathway, whereas those upregulated in non-survivors were enriched in the IL-17 pathway and other inflammatory and immune pathways. Integrated analysis revealed that the four tryptophan metabolites were associated with 20 differentially expressed proteins, six of which showed robust associations within outcome subgroups. Collectively, tryptophan metabolic disturbances coupled with inflammatory proteomic features may characterize fatal severe SFTS, and the identified metabolite-protein signatures may serve as promising prognostic biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets in critically ill patients.

Rabies immunoglobulin utilization and delayed presentation following category III rabies exposure: a 10-year retrospective study in Hangzhou, China.
BACKGROUND: Rabies is an almost invariably fatal, vaccine-preventable zoonosis. Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is recommended for Category III exposures, yet real-world RIG utilization remains poorly characterized. This study examined temporal trends and factors associated with RIG utilization and delayed presentation among Category III exposure patients in China. METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted using clinical records of Category III exposure patients presenting to a high-volume rabies prevention clinic in Hangzhou, China, from 2015 to 2024. Calendar year 2018 was treated as a temporal reference year for descriptive comparison. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with RIG non-administration and delayed presentation (>24 h post-exposure). RESULTS: A total of 14,270 eligible cases were analyzed. Overall RIG utilization was 37.54%, declining from 53.09% in 2015 to 7.14% in 2022. RIG non-administration was independently associated with male sex (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.11-1.29), age 18-59 years (OR 3.25, 95% CI 2.95-3.59), exposure at home (OR 1.47, 95% CI 1.33-1.63), presentation in 2018 (OR 2.38, 95% CI 2.01-2.82) and in 2019-2024 (OR 4.49, 95% CI 3.96-5.09), and delayed presentation (OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.32-1.55). The overall delayed presentation rate was 34.47%; independent risk factors included age 18-59 years (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.24-1.52), exposure at home (OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.41-1.74), and presentation in 2018 (OR 1.61, 95% CI 1.40-1.86) and in 2019-2024 (OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.62-1.94). CONCLUSION: RIG utilization was low and showed marked temporal variation during 2015-2024, and one third of patients presented more than 24 h after exposure. Both outcomes were concentrated among working-age adults and domestic exposure settings. These findings describe service utilization patterns and identify subgroups in which gaps in PEP delivery are concentrated; targeted risk communication and routine monitoring of RIG utilization and presentation timeliness are needed.

Diverse Staphylococcus aureus lineages in a tertiary hospital in North Central Nigeria: emergence of CC1-ST772-MRSA, CC8-ST789-MRSA, and ST152-MRSA.
INTRODUCTION: Staphylococcus aureus is a human pathogen associated with both hospital- and community-acquired infections. Data on its molecular epidemiology in North Central Nigeria are currently unavailable. This study investigated the antibiotic resistance, virulence genes, and the population structure of S. aureus in a tertiary hospital in North Central Nigeria. METHODS: S. aureus strains from various clinical specimens collected between July 2017 and July 2021 were characterized based on antibiotic susceptibility testing and PCR detection of nuc, mecA, PVL (lukS-PV/lukF-PV), and immune evasion (scn, sak, chp) genes. Genotyping of the strains was performed by spa typing and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of representative strains. RESULTS: Of the 169 S. aureus strains, 52% (n = 88) were recovered from wound infections. The resistance rates were highest for penicillin (n = 162; 96%), followed by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (n = 128; 76%), tetracycline (n = 66; 39%), gentamicin (n = 54; 32%), ciprofloxacin (n = 53; 31%), erythromycin (n = 31; 18%), and clindamycin (n = 3; 2%). Overall, 90 (53%) were mecA-positive (MRSA), and 81 strains (48%) were multidrug-resistant (MDR). Genotyping revealed a diverse S. aureus population, comprising 37 spa types and 19 sequence types (STs) in nine clonal complexes (CC1, CC5, CC8, CC15, CC22, CC30, CC45, CC88, CC121) and two singletons (ST152 and ST7572). The predominant MRSA lineages comprised CC1-ST772-MRSA-V-t657, CC8-ST789-MRSA-V-t091, and ST152-MRSA-Vc-t4690, while the common methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) lineages were ST152-MSSA-t355, CC15-ST15-MSSA-t084, and CC5-ST5-MSSA-t311. The dfrG gene was detected across lineages, and 65% of all strains (MSSA: 68%; MRSA: 62%) were PVL-positive. Phylogenetic analysis revealed strain diversity, suggesting the dissemination of different lineages across various wards within the hospital. CONCLUSION: The S. aureus population at a tertiary hospital in North-Central Nigeria is highly diverse. The detection of PVL-positive ST152-MRSA-Vc and MDR CC1-ST722-MRSA-V is of significant public health concern. Genomic surveillance of S. aureus, combined with clinical data, is essential for effective infection prevention and control strategies.

Genomic insights into multidrug and extensively drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae from bloodstream infections at three Zambian tertiary hospitals.
BACKGROUND: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of hospital-associated infections and a major contributor to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) worldwide. Despite its importance and prioritisation in Zambia's National Action Plan on AMR, genomic surveillance information in sub-Saharan Africa remains limited. This study investigated the population structure, determinants of AMR, and plasmid diversity of K. pneumoniae isolates from three tertiary hospitals in Zambia. METHODS: Thirty archived K. pneumoniae blood isolates collected between December 2023 and May 2025 from University Teaching Hospitals (UTH), Ndola University Teaching Hospital (NUTH), and Livingstone University Teaching Hospital (LUTH) and subjected to antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) and whole-genome sequencing (Illumina NextSeq 2000). Sequence types (STs), plasmid replicons, and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) were identified using MLST, PlasmidFinder, and the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database, respectively. RESULTS: Twenty-eight isolates (93%) were multidrug-resistant, of which seven (25%) were extensively drug-resistant (XDR), exhibiting resistance across eight antibiotic classes, including carbapenems. Whole-genome sequencing identified 18 sequence types (STs), including two novel STs, and globally disseminated high-risk clones such as ST11, ST15, ST101, ST307, ST377, and ST607, which are circulating across hospitals. UTH exhibited the highest diversity of STs. The seven XDR K. pneumoniae isolates, six (85%) were from UTH, while the remaining isolate was from NUTH. Among the XDR isolates, five belonged to clinically dominant clones, comprising ST377 (two isolates) and single representatives of ST101, ST307, and ST607. The other two were ST13 and ST831, which have not been reported to have an XDR profile. All isolates carried multiple ARGs, dominated by those encoding β-lactamases (bla CTX-M-15: 93%, bla TEM: 70%), aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (aac(6')-Ib-cr5: 77%, aac(3)-IIe: 64%), and efflux pump genes (emrD: 100%). The carbapenemase-encoding gene, bla NDM-5, was present in 13% of the isolates. CONCLUSIONS: This first genomic survey of K. pneumoniae in Zambia reveals extensive clonal diversity dominated by global high-risk lineages carrying plasmid-mediated ESBL and carbapenemase genes. The detection of XDR strains, particularly at UTH, underscores the urgent need to strengthen laboratory surveillance across all tertiary hospitals in Zambia and improve infection prevention programmes.

Characterization of pulmonary bacterial composition in community-acquired pneumonia depending on sampling methods.
INTRODUCTION: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) remains a major global health concern due to its high incidence, morbidity, mortality, and economic impact. Although Streptococcus pneumoniae is the primary bacterial cause, diverse bacterial and viral pathogens contribute to CAP etiology. Conventional microbiological methods provide limited characterization of the pulmonary microbiome, resulting in low diagnostic yield and frequent empirical antibiotic use. This pilot study aimed to characterize the pulmonary microbiome in adult CAP patients using high-throughput sequencing and to determine whether commonly used non-invasive samples accurately represent the lower respiratory tract. METHODS: Pulmonary samples were obtained using invasive procedures (bronchoalveolar lavage, bronchial aspirate, bronchial brushing, and biopsy) and non-invasive methods (sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate). Classical microbiological testing identified pathogens in 24.1% of cases. DNA extracted was subjected to 16S rRNA gene amplification and sequencing, and microbial composition and diversity were compared across sampling types. RESULTS: Microbiome profiles differed significantly by sampling methodology. Non-invasive samples displayed high variability and limited correspondence with lower airway microbiota. In contrast, invasive samples demonstrated greater consistency and appeared more representative of the lower respiratory tract. The genus Ralstonia was significantly more abundant in invasive samples (p < 0.05), warranting further investigation of its potential biological and clinical relevance. CONCLUSIONS: 16S rRNA gene sequencing provides comprehensive detection of pulmonary microorganisms and offers added value in the microbiological diagnosis of CAP. The findings highlight the importance of using invasive specimens for accurate microbiome characterization and for detecting bacterial taxa not identified by routine microbiological methods.

Adaptive laboratory evolution and proteomic insight on collateral sensitivity for meropenem in colistin-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae.
BACKGROUND: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global challenge, with an estimated ≥10 million deaths per year by 2050. Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae), a critical priority bacterial pathogen, is rapidly developing resistance even against next-generation (meropenem) and last-resort (colistin) antibiotics, whereas the pipeline for discovery and development of new antibiotic(s) for treatment of antibiotic-resistant K. pneumoniae infections is a lengthy, resource-intensive, and costly process and hence demands exploring alternative and effective treatment strategies. Capitalizing on the simultaneous emergence of collateral sensitivity (CS) to resistant antibiotics can therefore be a rapid and effective strategy to fill the gap. METHODS: Adaptive laboratory evolution was enforced in K. pneumoniae (American Type Culture Collection [ATCC] and clinical strains) by exposing it to sequentially increasing sub-lethal dosages (0.25, 0.5, and 1xMIC) of colistin and meropenem, and a panel of pathogens representing early (0.25xMIC), mid (0.5xMIC), and late (1xMIC) stages of emergence of AMR was developed. Similarly, colistin (1xMIC)-resistant K. pneumoniae cells were also adapted to develop resistance against meropenem. Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight (MALDI-TOF) for pathogen identification and VITEK-2 for antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) profiles validated resistant pathogens, which were then proteomic profiled to investigate CS between colistin and meropenem at both phenotypic and proteome levels. RESULTS: AST of developed panels revealed that colistin-resistant pathogens became sensitive to meropenem during adaptation to colistin, representing CS, which was validated by the emergence of colistin sensitivity when colistin-resistant K. pneumoniae adapted against meropenem. Proteomic analysis of the resistant panels identified a total of 3,126 proteins, including 23 and 5 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in colistin- and meropenem-resistant pathogens, respectively. Among these, 12 proteins (phoP, arnB/arnD/arnT, and pmrD/pmrA) (associated with two components: system regulator and antibiotic resistance); degP, kdpB, maeA, frmR, fhuC, and entF (responsible for virulence and stress adaptation); and fhuC, entF, and amn (required for iron acquisition and persistence) showed altered pattern matching along with CS, that is, upregulated during emergence of colistin resistance along with meropenem sensitivity and conversely downregulated during emergence of colistin sensitivity along with meropenem-resistance in colistin-1x resistant K. pneumoniae. CONCLUSION: This study, for the first time, developed a unique panel of colistin- and meropenem-resistant K. pneumoniae cells representing the early, mid, and late stages of AMR emergence. The simultaneous emergence of CS for meropenem while developing resistance against colistin among the panels may pave the way to devise antibiotic cycling and/or co-dosing approaches, and modulation of the expression of the identified 12 potential proteomic biomarkers may be utilized to regulate the emergence of CS for meropenem in colistin-resistant pathogens for combating colistin-resistant infections.

Whole-genome sequencing analysis of phylogenetic relationships and lineage diversity of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in Western Kenya.
BACKGROUND: Western Kenya remains a high-burden tuberculosis (TB) region, yet genomic data describing the diversity and phylogenetic relationships of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) strains are limited. Understanding sub-lineage patterns and the phylogenetic relationships is essential for effective TB surveillance and control strategies. METHODS: This was a cross-sectional whole genome sequencing (WGS) study using archived MTBC isolates from 12 counties in Western Kenya. Genomic DNA was extracted using a modified CTAB protocol and sequenced using the Element AVITI platform. Reads were processed using DuffyNGS/DuffyTools pipeline and aligned to the H37Rv reference genome. Lineages were assigned using TBProfiler v4.3.0 based on single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP). Phylogenetic relationships were reconstructed using Nextstrain and interpreted using tree topology. RESULTS: Of 316 MTBC isolates processed, 290 met quality criteria for WGS. Lineage 4 (L4) (42%) and Lineage 3 (L3) (38%) predominated, with significant county-level heterogeneity observed in Kisii and Homa Bay (L4), and Siaya and Migori (L3) (p < 0.0296). Sub-lineage analysis revealed widespread circulation of L2.2.1 and L3.1.1 strains, alongside substantial L4 diversity. Rare sub-lineages showed limited geographic distribution and one Mycobacterium bovis isolate was identified. Phylogenetic analysis revealed geographically structured relatedness, with a localized circulation in Kisii, broader regional distribution in Homa Bay, and additional clades showing intermediate regional patterns. CONCLUSION: Western Kenya harbors genetically diverse and spatially MTBC population with distinct patterns of phylogenetic relatedness. These findings demonstrate the value of WGS for characterizing population structure and informing targeted TB control in high-burden settings.

From listening to action: how social and behavioral evidence informed multisectoral cholera response in Zambia, 2023-2024.
Rapid qualitative assessments and community feedback mechanisms are increasingly recognized as core components of risk communication and community engagement in public health emergencies, yet few documented examples exist of how this evidence has directly influenced outbreak response decision-making. This case study examines the 2023-2024 cholera outbreak in Zambia, analyzing how social and behavioral data generated through multiple rounds of rapid qualitative assessment, alongside national community feedback mechanisms, informed multisectoral response activities. Drawing on document review, consultations with response pillar members, assessment reports, feedback dashboards, and triangulation with epidemiological data, the study traces how community concerns, rumors, beliefs, perceptions and priorities were collected, analyzed and applied across health, water, sanitation and hygiene, and protection response pillars. Enabling factors included pre-existing technical capacity, strong partnerships between government humanitarian actors, and academia, and rapid feedback loops that supported near real-time adaptation. Challenges at different points in the response included delayed resource allocation, uneven subnational coordination, and limited capacity to process large volumes of feedback data. The Zambia experience demonstrates that community-generated evidence can meaningfully influence outbreak response when integrated across response pillars rather than confined to behavioral interventions alone, representing a broader shift in public health practice that positions community perspectives as central to decision-making. This, in turn, strengthens effectiveness, trust, accountability, and transparency by aligning interventions with community-identified priorities. While grounded in the Zambian context, the findings are relevant for preparedness, anticipatory action, and response across a range of public health emergencies.

β-Glucan-mediated macrophage priming enhances macrophage activation and host defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
Tuberculosis remains a major cause of infectious mortality worldwide, highlighting the need for complementary therapeutic strategies beyond conventional antibiotics. Host-directed approaches may enhance macrophage-mediated control of infection. In this study, we investigated the effects of β-glucan priming combined with drug-loaded yeast-derived β-glucan particles (DYDGP) in an in vitro macrophage model of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA)-differentiated THP-1 macrophages were compared across unprimed, β-glucan-only, antibiotic-only, and β-glucan-primed/DYDGP-treated groups. β-Glucan priming combined with DYDGP treatment was associated with enhanced receptor-mediated phagocytic activity, improved intracellular bacterial control, and preserved macrophage integrity. These effects were associated with increased intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, enhanced phagolysosomal maturation, and altered autophagic activity. Colony-forming unit (CFU) analysis showed that β-glucan-primed macrophages treated with DYDGP exhibited a significantly lower bacterial burden than the unprimed, β-glucan-only, and antibiotic-only groups at 1, 6, and 24 h post-infection. Unprimed macrophages showed progressive bacterial growth, with log CFU values of 4.2, 4.8, and 5.2, whereas β-glucan-primed/DYDGP-treated macrophages showed reduced values of 3.3, 2.5, and 2.1, respectively. β-Glucan-only treatment resulted in log CFU values of 4.2, 4.4, and 4.7, while antibiotic-only treatment resulted in values of 4.2, 4.1, and 3.9 at the corresponding time points. These findings suggest that β-glucan priming combined with DYDGP treatment may enhance intracellular control of M. tuberculosis in this macrophage model and support further investigation of this approach as a potential adjunctive strategy for tuberculosis.

Case Report: Bacteremic respiratory tularemia causing refractory ARDS requiring VV-ECMO.
BACKGROUND: Respiratory tularemia is a rare but potentially serious manifestation of Francisella tularensis infection. We report a rare case of bacteremic respiratory tularemia complicated by refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) requiring veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO), highlighting the diagnostic challenges and therapeutic implications of this uncommon presentation. CASE PRESENTATION: A 78-year-old man developed severe pneumonia following river water aspiration after a bicycle accident. After transient initial improvement, he experienced progressive respiratory deterioration despite broad-spectrum antimicrobial treatment, ultimately developing refractory ARDS requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, prone positioning and VV-ECMO. Three consecutive sets of blood cultures revealed the presence of Francisella tularensis, whereas bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cultures remained negative. No extrapulmonary manifestations of tularemia were identified. Targeted antimicrobial therapy with ciprofloxacin and gentamicin was initiated but failed to prevent a fatal outcome. CONCLUSION: Respiratory tularemia should be considered in patients with severe pneumonia following environmental exposure, particularly when respiratory status deteriorates despite broad-spectrum β-lactam therapy. Repeated blood cultures may establish the diagnosis despite negative BAL cultures. Early recognition and prompt initiation of effective antimicrobial therapy are essential, as β-lactam antibiotics are clinically ineffective against F. tularensis. This case also illustrates the potential severity of respiratory tularemia, which may progress to refractory ARDS requiring VV-ECMO.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis Rv3248c Inhibits Type I Interferon Response and Promotes Intracellular Survival by Mediating Ubiquitin-Proteasome-Dependent Degradation of TBK1.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) is a leading cause of infectious disease mortality worldwide, and M. tb subverts host immunity to persist intracellularly. Type I interferon (IFN-I) modulates host defense during M. tb infection, but the mechanisms controlling their induction remain incompletely defined. In this research, a previously uncharacterized mycobacterial factor, M. tb Rv3248c, which regulates IFN-I response, was identified using pull-down and mass spectrometry. Overexpression of Rv3248c suppresses IFN-β expression in macrophages at both the transcriptional and protein levels. In addition, it also enhances intracellular bacterial load, whereas in bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) from Ifnar1-/- C57BL/6 mice, the difference of bacterial load was no longer statistically significant, suggesting that Rv3248c enhances mycobacterial survival in IFN-I-dependent manner. Furthermore, the study shows that M. tb Rv3248c inhibits IFN-I response via the cGAS-STING pathway. Mechanistically, Rv3248c binds TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) and promotes its ubiquitination-mediated proteasomal degradation. The N-terminal region of Rv3248c (amino acids 1-134) is required for TBK1 interaction and IFN-I inhibition. These findings identify a previously uncharacterized mechanism by which M. tb dampens the IFN-I response by targeting TBK1, highlighting Rv3248c as a contributor to pathogenesis and a potential therapeutic target.

Development of GuaB Inhibitors to Treat Mycobacterium tuberculosis Infection.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is responsible for more deaths per year than any other infectious disease. Resistance of circulating Mtb to the standard of care treatment regimen is an urgent global health crisis for which novel antibiotic treatments are needed. We have developed extremely potent, orally bioavailable, small-molecule inhibitors of inosine 5'-monophosphate dehydrogenase (GuaB) that catalyze the rate-limiting step in de novo guanine biosynthesis. The inhibitors exhibited bactericidal activity against Mtb in extracellular, intracellular, and hypoxic environments that capture features of advanced disease pathology in patients. Mtb GuaB2 inhibitors (GuaBi) were efficacious in three different in vivo mouse models of Mtb lung infection: the C57BL/6 super acute, C57BL/6 chronic, and C3HeB/FeJ (Kramnik) models. In the chronic BALB/c infection model of primarily intracellular Mtb, no benefit was observed, whereas in the C3HeB/FeJ model, a bedaquiline, pretomanid, and moxifloxacin treatment regimen that included GuaBi led to a rapid elimination of culturable Mtb infection in half of the mice. Notably, the C3HeB/FeJ model recapitulates advanced pathophysiology and heterogeneous disease that includes caseous necrotic granulomas, intracellular and extracellular reservoirs of Mtb, and lethal progressive infection. These results support further evaluation of a GuaBi-containing therapeutic regimen in relapse-capable preclinical models.

Challenges and Advances in Elucidating the Electronic Circular Dichroism of Crystalline Materials through First-Principles Calculations.
The electronic circular dichroism (ECD) of crystalline materials is governed by physical effects that are absent in isolated-molecule theory. Bloch-state delocalization makes position-operator matrix elements ill-defined and requires Berry-connection formulations of the periodic optical-activity response, while excitonic effects redistribute oscillator strength across the band gap. This Perspective critically surveys the hierarchy of first-principles methods that have been established to address these challenges. Molecular-cluster time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) provides chemical intuition and mechanistic insight but cannot represent the complete periodic response and can underestimate long-range crystal field effects. Periodic independent-particle calculations incorporate the crystalline environment and band-geometric response, whereas self-consistent coupled-perturbed approaches additionally include crystal-orbital relaxation. Adaptive Brillouin-zone sampling can accelerate convergence for localized one-particle contributions, although nonuniform meshes complicate momentum conservation in the correlated treatments. GW-BSE provides a rigorous framework for excitonic optical activity, whereas maximally localized Wannier function interpolation efficiently converges the DFT-level periodic quantities used to analyze the band-geometric response. A generally validated workflow that combines the BSE-level excitonic response with all geometric and interpolation ingredients has not yet been established. Finally, we discuss open challenges including fully relativistic treatments of chiral rare-earth halide perovskites and single-crystal anisotropy measurements.

Buffaloed in Brandenburg: Germany's first brush with foot-and-mouth disease after four decades of freedom.
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) virus is one of the most feared and most consequential pathogens of livestock worldwide. It can be spread rapidly by the transboundary movement of animals, animal products, and by-products. In January 2025, Germany detected its first FMD outbreak since 1988 in extensively reared water buffalo on a small farm in the state of Brandenburg, directly outside Berlin, the federal capital. Immediate control measures including a standstill for movements of susceptible animals and pre-emptive culling were implemented by the veterinary authorities. Whole-genome sequencing identified the virus as serotype O, topotype ME-SA, lineage SA-2018 and revealed extensive recombination, but cross-neutralization assays suggested good heterologous protection by an O/PanAsia-2 vaccine strain. Epidemiological back-calculation placed the time of virus introduction in late December 2024. Although the entry route remains unresolved, human-associated introduction is most likely. Network analysis revealed minimal farm connectivity, and simulations predicted low potential for onward transmission, which is consistent with the outbreak being ultimately restricted to a single herd. This event underscores the constant and unpredictable risk of introduction of the virus. Early detection through increased awareness and comprehensive differential diagnostics as well as the international collaboration of veterinary services, laboratories, and experts are essential in the face of the global presence of FMD.

Nowcasting officially reported highly pathogenic avian influenza outbreak counts under heterogeneous reporting delays.
Official animal disease series are often incomplete due to delays in reporting. This retrospective observational study evaluated whether increased model complexity enhances probabilistic nowcasts of eventual officially reported outbreak-equivalent counts. We reconstructed historical information states from a fixed extraction from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) World Animal Health Information System (WAHIS), which included 46,860 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) and 72,690 African swine fever (ASF) outbreaks. Twelve prespecified methods were assessed over 78 locked cutoffs for 2024-2025 using the Weighted Interval Score (WIS), calibration diagnostics, block bootstrap, simulation, and a separately frozen USDA APHIS transfer evaluation. The primary HPAI analysis included 35,880 observations from 115 country-host units. At week closure, only 7.6% of eventual HPAI and 6.7% of ASF outbreak equivalents were visible, with completeness varying by host, region, year, season, and workload. The prespecified primary hypothesis was not supported: the delay-aware temporal network scored 6.9% worse than the hierarchical Bayesian comparator, and the relational graph changed WIS by only 0.4%. Gradient-boosted quantile regression improved WIS by 18.5% (absolute difference -0.0397, 95% interval -0.0553 to -0.0255), but the improvement reached 26.0% among high-volume reporters and reversed to a 6.3% deficit among units with minimal reporting history. Conditioning on the partial count was 24.7% worse than a matched no-delay network at cohort age 0 and performed better thereafter. The slower-reporting ASF system reversed the pooled contrast, whereas the APHIS module improved WIS by 10.1% after system-specific retraining. Adding an explicit mass at zero enhanced the transparent comparator by 18.8% and resulted in no detectable difference from gradient boosting; the neural model remained 17.4% worse under the same recalibration. In exploratory analyses, gradient boosting cleared the prespecified 5% gate under all six cohort definitions and all three maturity horizons. Performance deteriorated markedly for high-volume countries and regions excluded from training. These estimates pertain to eventual officially reported outbreak equivalents under the surveillance conditions studied, not undetected infections.

Pattern recognition receptors and divergent disease severity in zoonotic viral infections.
Zoonotic viruses continue to emerge unpredictably, cross species barriers, and inflict major health, economic, and ecological burdens. Recent outbreaks of SARS-CoV-2, H5N1 avian influenza virus (AIV), monkeypox, and Zika virus underscore the unpredictability of viral emergence and the urgent need to understand host/pathogen interactions. This review focuses on how innate immune sensing via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) shapes disease severity across different species. While PRRs initiate antiviral defenses (interferons, ISGs), inflammatory cytokines, and programmed cell death, host outcomes diverge widely, shaped by genetic variation in PRR pathways and their regulators. Dysregulated inflammatory responses and inflammatory cell death can contribute substantially to severe disease independently of viral load, as demonstrated in influenza and coronavirus infections. Viral effectors that suppress or alter PRR signaling can show species-specific efficacy, and these mismatches can be critical determinants of disease when viruses jump hosts. Using avian influenza as an example, we highlight how disease outcomes vary with viral strain, host species, response timing, and tissue context. Overall, we propose that differential disease severity across host species reflects the balance among PRR-mediated resistance, the efficiency of viral immune evasion in the relevant host, and innate disease-tolerance mechanisms that limit tissue damage. Understanding these dynamics could enhance our ability to predict zoonotic emergence and mitigate the impact of viral pandemics.

Genetic characterization of highly similar H9N2 viruses isolated from swine and poultry in China.
H9N2 avian influenza viruses (AIVs) are widely distributed in poultry and have attracted continued attention because of their high reassortment potential and ability to cross species barriers. In March 2019, two H9N2 viruses were isolated from a pig and a chicken, respectively, in Shandong Province, China. In this study, we characterized the whole-genome features, phylogenetic relationships, molecular characteristics, and pathogenicity of the two viruses in mice. Whole-genome sequence analysis showed that the eight gene segments of the two isolates shared 99.9%-100% nucleotide sequence identity. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the two viruses had the same reassortant genomic composition, with the HA and NA genes related to the Y280-like lineage, the PB2 and M genes related to the G1-like lineage, and the PB1, PA, NP, and NS genes related to the SH/F98-like lineage. According to the historical H9N2 genotype nomenclature, both viruses were classified as G57 and were genetically closely related to H9N2 viruses previously detected in environmental samples in Jiangsu Province, China. Several amino acid substitutions previously associated with mammalian adaptation, receptor binding, viral replication, and antigenic variation were identified in both isolates; however, their biological effects were not experimentally evaluated in this study. In mice, both viruses replicated in the lungs and nasal turbinates and caused interstitial pneumonia, but neither virus caused significant body weight loss or death, and no virus was detected in the liver, spleen, kidney, or brain. Overall, the two H9N2 viruses isolated from a pig and a chicken showed highly similar whole-genome characteristics and shared several molecular features previously associated with mammalian adaptation. However, given the limited number of isolates and the lack of direct epidemiological and transmission evidence, the present study does not provide sufficient evidence to establish direct poultry-to-swine transmission, the direction of transmission, or sustained cross-species transmission.

H5 influenza virus mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccination elicits adaptive immune responses in Holstein calves.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 circulated widely in lactating dairy cows in the United States following the initial detection in 2024. Due to the critical need for intervention strategies for this outbreak, we evaluated antibody and cellular immune responses of a clade 2.3.4.4b H5 mRNA-LNP vaccine in calves. We found that the H5 mRNA-LNP vaccine induced a robust antibody and CD8+ T cell-mediated immune response and conferred protection against clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 infection.IMPORTANCEIt is important to develop vaccines that limit clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 infection in cattle. In this study, we found that a new H5 mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine is immunogenic when delivered intramuscularly to male Holstein calves.

Mathematical modeling of in vitro replication dynamics for multiple highly pathogenic avian influenza clade 2.3.4.4 viruses in chicken and duck cells.
The introduction, spread, and subsequent detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) in poultry are influenced by the virus replication fitness, transmission fitness, and virulence. Quantifying these fitness parameters is important for implementing surveillance and control measures for poultry. This study employs an avian in vitro model using primary chicken embryo fibroblast and duck embryo fibroblast to identify cellular correlates of fitness for a reference panel of eight dominant, highly pathogenic avian influenza clade 2.3.4.4 virus genotypes (H5N1, H5N8, and H5N6) isolated between 2014 and 2024. Because HPAIVs are pantropic in poultry, the use of primary fibroblasts could provide a robust systemic model to assess virus fitness in different poultry species. By integrating longitudinal infectious virus titers and cytopathogenicity data with a mathematical model, which delineates cell populations into susceptible, latent, infectious, and dead compartments, we disentangled "traditional" virological parameters such as peak virus titer and time to 50% cell death from mechanistic parameters, including the infecting time ([Formula: see text]), generation time ([Formula: see text]), and basic reproduction number (R0). Our results confirm host-specific fitness characteristics consistent with in vivo observations. This study underscores the potential of integrating avian in vitro models with mathematical modeling to provide high-resolution characterization of genetically similar viruses, building toward rapid risk assessments of novel HPAIVs.IMPORTANCEHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) outbreaks in poultry have resulted in the culling of millions of animals over the past decade. The introduction and spread of HPAI in poultry are driven by the ability of the virus to replicate, transmit, and cause disease, which varies among different poultry species. These viral fitness traits can change quickly through mutations or reassortment, leading to new variants with an altered risk of introduction and transmission. In this study, we integrated an in vitro and mathematical model to assess the viral fitness of genetically similar viruses and the risk they represent for two important poultry species. This approach offers a rapid and scalable alternative to traditional animal models, aligning with the 3R's principle and supporting rapid assessment of the viral fitness of emerging virus variants for poultry. This approach can be easily expanded to other species, including humans, and is suitable to assess the viral fitness of all viral pathogens.

A comparison of health care utilization among insured working-age adults in the state of Virginia, U.S. by long COVID and disabling condition status in 2022.
OBJECTIVE: Americans with disabilities experience more medical interactions and greater access barriers than those without. After the COVID-19 pandemic, Long COVID (LCOVID) emerged as a chronic condition. Few studies examine patterns among people with disabling conditions who develop LCOVID. This study compared healthcare utilization rates among individuals with and without LCOVID and/or a potentially disabling condition (PDC) among working-age adults in Virginia's insurance plans in 2022. METHODS: Retrospective analysis using 2021-22 administrative claims data from Virginia's All-Payer Claims Database estimated rates of primary, emergency, and inpatient care among adults aged 18-64 with PDC(s) and LCOVID. Disabling conditions were identified using specifications from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and LCOVID was identified using the ICD-10 code U09.9. Members were grouped by PDC/LCOVID status, sex and age. We applied regression models to estimate rates and compare differences across diagnostic groups. RESULTS: Among most groups, individuals with both PDCs and LCOVID had the highest rates of primary, emergency, and inpatient utilization. Those with LCOVID or PDC alone also often had higher utilization than those with neither. CONCLUSION: These findings underscore the need for accessible, cost-effective care for people with disabling conditions and Long COVID.

Determinants of preventive Chinese herbal medicine use: an extended health belief model analysis and its nursing implications.
BACKGROUND: The COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed global interest in traditional health practices. In Taiwan, Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) emerged as a key component of preventive care; yet, its psychological adoption mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. This study evaluated an extended Health Belief Model (HBM) to elucidate these cognitive associations. OBJECTIVE: To examine factors associated with preventive CHM adoption among Taiwanese adults during the COVID-19 Omicron wave and evaluate the mediating role of cues to action within the HBM framework. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted (January-December 2022) with 499 Taiwanese adults. Multivariable linear regression and Hayes' PROCESS Macro (Model 4) path mediation analysis were executed, adjusting for five socio-demographic covariates (age, gender, education, healthcare professional status, and Hualien residence). RESULTS: Preventive CHM behavior correlated significantly with cues to action ( r = 0.588 , p < 0.001 ) and perceived benefits ( r = 0.519 , p < 0.001 ). Covariate-adjusted regression identified cues to action ( B = 0.369 , p < 0.001 ) and perceived barriers ( B = - 0.095 , p = 0.008 ) as independent predictors, accounting for 34.4 % of total variance ( R 2 = 0.344 ). Crucially, cues to action fully mediated the statistical relationship between perceived benefits and behavior (indirect effect = 0.351 , 95 % Bootstrap CI [ 0.236 , 0.478 ] ; direct path p = 0.726 ). Significant subgroup variations emerged among healthcare professionals, individuals with chronic conditions ( 24.4 % ), and Hualien residents. CONCLUSION: Health beliefs-specifically perceived benefits catalyzed via cues to action-are pivotally associated with CHM adoption. Nursing administrators should leverage these insights to design culturally tailored health communication, empower nurses as institutional triggers, and establish structured safety screening for chronic disease cohorts regarding potential herb-drug interactions.

Party capacity, state capacity, and pandemic governance: a fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis of COVID-19 prevention and control outcomes in 52 African countries during the early stage.
INTRODUCTION: During the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in Africa, from March to May 2020, significant variations emerged among countries regarding the implementation of containment policies. During this period, viewed strictly from a public health perspective, social distancing and lockdowns were considered critical for curbing transmission. However, epidemic control outcomes varied considerably across countries. This variation raises questions about the independent and interactive influence of socioeconomic conditions on these outcomes, and about how political factors, including state capacity and party politics, moderate or mediate these influences, especially in resource-constrained contexts. METHODS: This article employs fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) with 52 African countries as case studies to investigate the combination of conditions for COVID-19 containment success. RESULTS: The analysis reveals three equifinal configurations: a party-led high-risk response pathway, an administrative compensation pathway, and a coercive compensation pathway. Party capacity is not a generally applicable determinant; its role is contingent upon the specific governance context. Under the structural constraint of healthcare deficiency, distinct dimensions of state capacity operate through differentiated compensatory mechanisms. DISCUSSION: The paper makes two theoretical contributions: conceptualizing party capacity as a crisis-contingent rather than a generalized governance asset, and disaggregating state capacity into administrative and coercive dimensions with distinct compensatory functions. It also makes a methodological contribution by adopting a configurational approach that examines combinations of conditions rather than the net effects of individual factors.

Knowledge, trust, and multidimensional perceptions of human papillomavirus vaccination among women attending a single primary care centre in Astana, Kazakhstan: a cross-sectional study.
BACKGROUND: Kazakhstan reintroduced human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination in 2024, making public confidence and communication important. This study described HPV knowledge and trust in information sources and exploratorily examined vaccine-perception structure and correlates among women attending primary care in Astana. METHODS: A cross-sectional electronic survey was conducted from 17 January to 28 February 2026 among 221 adult women recruited through convenience sampling. HPV knowledge, source-specific trust, and 16 perception items were assessed. Exploratory psychometric analysis used polychoric correlations, parallel analysis, and principal-axis factor analysis with oblimin rotation to derive preliminary composite measures. Spearman correlations and robust multivariable linear models examined safety concern and perceived effectiveness. A secondary logistic model examined refusal or intention to refuse HPV vaccination for a daughter. RESULTS: Mean HPV knowledge was 4.95 ± 3.84 of 12. A five-item safety concern measure (mean 2.34 ± 0.97; α = 0.868; ω = 0.901) and a three-item perceived effectiveness measure (mean 3.20 ± 1.24; α = 0.922; ω = 0.948) were derived. Knowledge correlated negatively with safety concern (ρ = -0.284, p < 0.001) and positively with perceived effectiveness (ρ = 0.393, p < 0.001). Safety concern was associated with COVID-19 controversy spillover (B = 0.190, 95% CI 0.043-0.337), earlier-programme distrust (B = 0.197, 95% CI 0.047-0.347), and preference for natural immunity (B = 0.137, 95% CI 0.040-0.234). Higher knowledge (B = 0.061, 95% CI 0.010-0.111) and professional/scientific trust (B = 0.297, 95% CI 0.114-0.480) were associated with greater perceived effectiveness. Forty-nine participants (22.2%) reported refusal or intention to refuse vaccination for a daughter; knowing someone believed to have become seriously ill after vaccination was associated with this response (aOR 7.42, 95% CI 2.60-21.16). CONCLUSION: HPV vaccine perceptions were multidimensional. Knowledge and professional-scientific trust were linked mainly to perceived effectiveness, whereas safety concerns were more strongly related to vaccine narratives. Communication strategies should combine factual education with transparent safety dialogue and clinician communication.

Creating online cognitive assessment platform for children's literacy and math skills: a case study illustrated with the ACE kids platform.
Computerized versions of paper-and-pencil tests made behavioral assessments of children more automatic and precise. The COVID-19 pandemic further demonstrated the need for assessments to be offered online to allow for remote data collection.
